# Deployment

---

## Deploy Yano X

Source: https://yano-x.io/deployment/

> Start with a local demonstration, rehearse a shared application on one machine, then set it up for real with the other operators.

Start with a local demonstration, rehearse a shared application on one
machine, then set it up for real with the other operators.

| Your goal | Start here | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| See Yano X working | [Local showcase](https://yano-x.io/start-here/quickstart/) | Three nodes, useful data, proofs, and a console |
| Rehearse a shared application | [`./yano.sh appchain try`](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/#1-practise-on-one-machine) | Every real setup step, on one machine, with three simulated operators |
| Run an application with other operators | [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/) | Each operator runs their own node; everyone checks they have the same chain |
| Add or remove a member, or add another application | [Grow and change it](https://yano-x.io/deployment/add-chain/) | One command per operator, without resetting anything |
| Run your node on a server | [Run your node on a server](https://yano-x.io/deployment/operators/) | A systemd service, open ports, and the cloud route for the showcase |

Yano X is JVM-only and requires Java 25. Yano's tooling calls an app ledger an
*app chain*, so commands and files say `appchain`.

#### Who does what

A real app ledger is run by several organizations. Each one is an
**operator**: it runs one member node and holds that node's private key, which
never leaves its machine. One person, the **coordinator**, defines the
application and collects everyone's public member card. The coordinator is
usually also an operator. The first operator listed is the **lead**.

Only public files travel between people: the draft, the member cards, and the
sealed `.chain` file. Send them however you like, or let
[join links](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/#easier-hand-out-join-links) carry them. Everyone
checks they have the same chain by comparing a short **chain fingerprint** on
a call.

An application can hold several chains. Each chain keeps its own genesis,
state, and finality history, and all of them run on the same member nodes.

#### Nodes, chains, and ports

Each node has one HTTP port and one node-to-node (n2n) port, however many
chains it hosts.

<!-- illustration: topology-ports -->

| How you run it | HTTP | Node-to-node | Change it with |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local showcase (`showcase.sh`) | `7070` + node index | `13337` + node index | `--http-base`, `--server-base` |
| `./yano.sh appchain try` | first free from `8080` | first free from `13337` | chosen for you and printed |
| One node per operator | `8080` on each host | `13337` on each host | `request --http-port`, `--node-port` |

`try` skips busy ports and prints the ones it chose. The showcase passes its
ports explicitly, so it stops instead. While the
coordinator hands out join links, `invite --serve` also listens on port `7099`
(`--port` changes it), which the operators must be able to reach.

#### Where to start

The supported evaluation posture is a local devnet. Public networks follow the
same steps, but anchoring and settlement there are explicit operations that
spend real test ADA; easier setup does not change
the release-readiness assessment.

**Next:** [start the local showcase](https://yano-x.io/start-here/quickstart/), or
[rehearse a shared application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/#1-practise-on-one-machine).

---

## Grow and change your application

Source: https://yano-x.io/deployment/add-chain/

> The new member finalizes blocks with the others, and no chain was reset.

- **Goal:** add or remove a member of a running application, recover from a
  lost key, host another application on the same nodes, and upgrade a node.
- **Before you start:** a live application from
  [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/), with every existing operator able to
  run one command on their own node.
- **Time:** a few minutes per operator; each change waits for the chain to
  make about ten blocks.
- **Outcome:** the new member finalizes blocks with the others, and no chain
  was reset.

Members are fixed at seal, but a `governed` application (the default) can
change them later. Every existing operator runs `approve` once; it does the
whole quorum-safe procedure on every chain of the application.

<!-- illustration: member-change -->
1. **Request.** The new operator runs `request supply.chain` and sends the
   card to every existing operator.
2. **Approve.** Each existing operator runs `approve dave.member` once, in any
   order.
3. **Raise the threshold.** If the new member count needs it, `approve` first
   raises the threshold and waits until that is active.
4. **Add.** It then adds the member and waits until that is active.
5. **Restart.** It adds the new peer to the operator's node and restarts the
   node once.
6. **Join and start.** The new operator runs `join supply.chain` and `start`;
   the node catches up.
<!-- /illustration -->

#### Add a member

The new operator, dave, needs the same Yano X release and the sealed
`supply.chain` file. On his machine:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain request supply.chain
```

> **✓ You should see** `✓ Wrote ./dave.member  (key id ee22fe112c2e69cb, …)`
> and `Next: send dave.member to the existing operators`.

Each existing operator, with their node running, then runs:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain approve dave.member
```

> **✓ You should see**
>
> ```text
> Adding dave (key ee22fe112c2e69cb, 127.0.0.1:15450) to supply
> orders: first raising the threshold from 2 to 3 (4 members)
> orders: waiting for threshold 3 (it activates once enough operators approve and the chain makes 10 more blocks)
> ✓ orders: dave is a member
> Restarting this node to connect to dave …
> ```

Check the key id against the one dave reads out to you before you approve.

- **Why the threshold rises.** Two of three is a majority; two of four is not.
  So while a three-member application grows, it runs at three of four for a
  while, and one offline member stops it. `approve` refuses to raise the
  threshold unless enough members are online.
- **Why it waits.** A change activates ten blocks after enough operators
  approve, and a chain only makes blocks when it has messages. On an idle
  `ordered-log`, `kv-registry`, or `approvals` chain, `approve` offers to send
  small heartbeat messages (`--heartbeat` in scripts); on an ordered log each
  one is a permanent entry. Other chains need ordinary traffic.
- **Safe to run again.** If `approve` is interrupted or times out, run it
  again: it skips what is done and reports what is still waiting.
  Approvals expire after 600 blocks.

When every operator has approved, dave joins and starts:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain join supply.chain
./yano.sh appchain start
./yano.sh appchain status supply
```

> **✓ You should see** four members online and `members agree` for every
> chain. Before every operator has approved, dave's status shows
> `waiting for approval`.

#### Remove a member

Each remaining operator runs:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain approve --remove carol
```

`approve` lowers the threshold if needed, removes carol on every chain, drops
her as a peer, and restarts the operator's node once. With `sequencing:
fixed` (the default) the lead cannot be removed: the runtime refuses to
remove the fixed proposer. An application sealed with `sequencing: rotating`
has no fixed proposer, so its lead can be removed like any other member
(on a devnet the lead's node still produces the Cardano devnet).

#### Recover from a lost key

If carol loses her node directory, **remove her first, then add her again**:

1. The other operators each run `approve --remove carol`. The chain keeps
   finalizing without her.
2. Carol makes a fresh node directory and runs `request supply.chain`, which
   creates a new key and card.
3. The others run `approve carol.member`; carol runs `join supply.chain` and
   `start`.

Adding first would raise the threshold to a level the lost key can never help
reach. With fixed sequencing the lead's key is the exception: losing it
means sealing a new application, so the lead must back up their node
directory.

#### Host another application on the same node

An operator can run several applications on one node. Each one is a separate
setup: the coordinator runs `new` and `seal` for it, and each operator runs
`request` and `join` with the new files. In an existing node directory,
`request` reuses your member key and addresses. Adding a chain to a running node
still needs a stop and start:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain join documents.chain
./yano.sh appchain stop
./yano.sh appchain start
```

`join` refuses a chain id the node already runs, and node-wide settings that
differ from those of the applications it already hosts. On a devnet, the
applications on one node must share the same lead.

A chain's state machines are fixed at its genesis. To add a new chain to an
existing application, seal a new application with the same operators.

#### Upgrade Yano X on a node

`start` checks the plugin bundles against the ones the node accepted at
`join`. After installing a newer Yano X release, it refuses with
`Plugin bundles changed since this node joined supply`. Agree the upgrade with
the other operators first, then accept the new bundles:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain join supply.chain --accept-bundles
./yano.sh appchain start
```

`join --accept-bundles` lists the changed bundles and records the new set.
Once every node runs again, the `Plugins:` line of `status` must show the same
catalog fingerprint on every member.
Changing what a state machine computes is a consensus change, not a rolling
upgrade; see [consensus rules](https://yano-x.io/plugins/consensus-rules/#evolving-a-live-chain).

#### Change an address

A peer's address is outside the chain fingerprint, so it can change without a
new chain. If bob moves, each other operator runs:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain join supply.chain --peer bob=node-b.example:13337
./yano.sh appchain stop && ./yano.sh appchain start
```

#### Troubleshooting

| You see | What it means and what to do |
|---|---|
| `This node must be running; run  yano.sh appchain start  first` | `approve` talks to your own node. Start it first. |
| `orders: only 2 members are connected, but the new threshold needs 3; bring the others online first so the chain cannot stall` | Ask the offline operators to start their nodes, then run `approve` again. |
| `orders: still waiting for …` and exit code 3 | The chain has not made enough blocks yet, or other operators have not approved. Send traffic, or run again later. |
| `dave.member was made for another application (invite …)` | The card was made for a different `.chain`. Ask dave to run `request supply.chain`. |
| `alice is the fixed proposer of orders; the runtime refuses to remove it.` | With fixed sequencing the lead cannot be removed. Losing the lead's key means sealing a new application. |

**Next:** [run your node on a server](https://yano-x.io/deployment/operators/).

---

## Set up an application with other operators

Source: https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/

> A live application whose members all agree, and a message that every node has finalized.

- **Goal:** run your own application with other organizations, each running
  their own node, and check that everyone has the same chain.
- **Before you start:** every operator needs the same extracted Yano X JVM
  release and Java 25 (or the self-contained edition for their platform, which
  bundles Java), and `curl`. For the message check at the end you also need
  `jq`.
- **Time:** 10 minutes for the rehearsal; about 30 minutes with real
  operators, most of it sending files and one short call.
- **Outcome:** a live application whose members all agree, and a message that
  every node has finalized.

There are two roles. The **coordinator** defines the application. Each
**operator** runs one member node; the coordinator is usually one of them.
Run every command from the extracted Yano X directory, the one that contains
`yano.sh`.

<!-- illustration: setup-ceremony -->
1. **New.** The coordinator runs `new`, which writes `supply.draft.yaml`, and
   sends it to every operator.
2. **Request.** Each operator runs `request supply.draft.yaml`, which makes
   their key and a member card such as `alice.member`, and sends the card back.
3. **Seal.** The coordinator puts the cards beside the draft and runs `seal`,
   which writes `supply.chain` and prints the chain fingerprint.
4. **Join.** On a call, everyone compares the fingerprint and each key id.
   Each operator then runs `join supply.chain` and confirms.
5. **Start.** Each operator runs `start`. On a devnet the lead starts first.
6. **Status.** Anyone runs `status supply` and sees `Live`.
<!-- /illustration -->

Every command ends with a `Next:` line that says what to do next. Add `--help`
to any command to see its options.

#### 1. Practise on one machine

`try` runs every real step on this machine, with one coordinator and three
simulated operators (alice, bob and carol), each in their own directory under
`./appchain-try/`. It prints each command as it runs it, so you can read along.

```bash
./yano.sh appchain try
```

> **✓ You should see** the seven numbered steps, then a message finalized at the
> same height and root on every node:
>
> ```text
>   alice  height 1  root 3d7d41336074db26…
>   bob    height 1  root 3d7d41336074db26…
>   carol  height 1  root 3d7d41336074db26…
> ✓ Message 53c00fd815014ae5… is final at height 1 on every node
> ```

Look around before you clean up:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain status --node-dir appchain-try/alice/yano-node
./yano.sh appchain try --clean     # stops the three nodes and deletes appchain-try/
```

`try --clean` deletes only its own rehearsal directory.

To rehearse your own chains, give `try` the same `--chain` and `--answer`
values as `new`. Without them it uses one `orders=audit-log` chain. The final
message check runs when one of the chains uses `audit-log`.

```bash
./yano.sh appchain try --chain orders=audit-log --chain registry=owned-registry
./yano.sh appchain try --chain flow=bindings:flow.yaml
```

**Prefer a browser?** `./yano.sh appchain ui` opens a page on this computer
(127.0.0.1 only) with the same steps: create (topic policies included), member
cards, seal, compare and join, start, status, approve, topic votes and anchor.
A progress bar shows where the application is, and once this node has joined,
its live dashboard comes first. Every button runs the command shown under it,
so the files are the same as from the terminal. The page can vote on a topics
plan you received; planning and signing stay in the terminal with their keys.

#### 2. The coordinator creates the draft

```bash
./yano.sh appchain new supply
```

A short wizard asks for the Cardano network, the operator names (you first),
and each chain: its id, and whether it runs one ready-made state machine
(a *recipe*) or several working together. If a recipe needs answers, such as
the genesis address of an `eutxo-ledger` chain, the wizard asks for each one.
`./yano.sh appchain recipes` lists the recipes and the answers each needs. To
skip the wizard, pass everything as flags, with one `--answer
<chain>.<name>=<value>` per answer:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain new supply --network devnet --operators alice,bob,carol \
  --chain orders=audit-log --yes
```

> **✓ You should see** `✓ Wrote ./supply.draft.yaml`, the invite code, the
> operators with the lead, and how many signatures each block needs.

The draft is a YAML file you can edit until you seal it:

```yaml
name: supply
invite: 7c1e-52aa-9d03            # written by `new`; do not edit
network: devnet                   # devnet | preview | preprod | mainnet
operators: [alice, bob, carol]    # the first is the lead
threshold: majority               # signatures per block: majority | two-thirds | all | a number
membership: governed
sequencing: fixed                 # fixed: the lead proposes every block | rotating: members take turns
chains:
  - id: orders                    # one state machine, chosen by recipe
    recipe: audit-log
  - id: approvals                 # several state machines joined by bindings
    recipe: declarative-composite
    bindings: ./approvals.bindings.yaml
    anchor: {mode: script, every-blocks: 10}   # optional anchor policy
    topics:                       # optional: namespaces and writer policies
      create: members             # who creates namespaces: members (vote) | registrars | anyone
      unregistered: open          # messages on topics no namespace covers: open | reject
```

- **The lead** is the first operator. On a devnet its node also produces the
  Cardano devnet. With `sequencing: fixed` (the default) the lead's node
  proposes every block, and the lead cannot be removed later, so the lead must
  back up their node directory.
- **Sequencing** chooses who proposes blocks. `fixed` keeps one proposer, the
  lead. `rotating` (`new --sequencing rotating`) lets the members take turns
  over Cardano slot windows, so no chain depends on one proposer, and
  `approve --remove` can then remove the lead too. On a devnet the lead's node
  still produces the Cardano devnet either way.
- **The threshold** is how many members must sign each block. With three
  operators, `majority` means two. While a chain grows by one member, it
  briefly needs one more signature.
- **A composite chain** runs several state machines that commit together.
  Create one with `--chain flow=bindings:<file>`, or choose "several" in the
  wizard and pick a starter; `new` copies the bindings file next to the draft.
  See [declarative bindings](https://yano-x.io/bindings/).
- **Topic policies** (`topics:`) let a chain give each namespace owners, a
  writer policy and a payload schema, and let users write through short-lived
  session keys. `create` says who creates a top-level namespace: the members
  by a vote (`members`), named operators or keys (`registrars: [alice]`), or
  anyone first come (`anyone`); members can always create and recover one by
  vote. `new --topics approvals=members` writes the block, and the wizard asks
  once per chain. It needs `membership: governed` and is fixed at seal. Keep
  `unregistered: open` unless every topic must be registered: a chain that
  refuses unregistered topics makes blocks only from registered traffic. See
  [protect a topic](#optional-protect-topics).
- **Answers** a recipe needs sit under the chain as `answers:`; `new --answer
  ledger.eutxoGenesisLovelace=100000000` writes the same thing. Answers are
  public: never put a secret in the draft.

Send `supply.draft.yaml` to every operator, including yourself, or hand out
join links instead (next section). Once operators have made cards, do not run
`new --force`: a new invite code makes their cards invalid.

#### Easier: hand out join links

Steps 3 to 5 below pass three kinds of file around by hand: the draft out,
the cards back, the sealed file out again. A join link carries all three. The
coordinator serves the draft for a limited time:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain invite supply.draft.yaml --serve --host coord.example.com
```

`--host` is the address the operators reach the coordinator's machine at
(default port `7099`; change it with `--port`, and open it to the operators).
The links stay valid for 24 hours (`--expires-hours`).

> **✓ You should see** one link per operator:
>
> ```text
> Serving supply.draft.yaml on port 7099 until 2026-10-28 09:14 UTC. Send each operator their link:
>   alice        yano.sh appchain request yano://coord.example.com:7099/5f0c…#7c1e-52aa-9d03
>   bob          yano.sh appchain request yano://coord.example.com:7099/a91d…#7c1e-52aa-9d03
>   carol        yano.sh appchain request yano://coord.example.com:7099/03be…#7c1e-52aa-9d03
> ```

Send each operator their own line. Each operator runs it (with their own
`--host`, ports and other `request` options as in step 3):

```bash
./yano.sh appchain request 'yano://coord.example.com:7099/5f0c…#7c1e-52aa-9d03' --host node-a.example.com
```

The command fetches the draft, makes the key and card, sends the card to the
coordinator, and waits. When every card is in, the coordinator's terminal asks
`Seal now?` (`invite --serve --seal` seals without asking). Each waiting
`request` then saves `supply.chain` and, in a terminal, continues straight into
`join`, which asks you to confirm the fingerprint and key ids as in step 5. The
listener stops once every operator has the sealed file.

`request <link> --no-wait` sends the card and returns; run the same command
again later to receive the sealed file, and running it again after an
interruption resumes. Each link works for one operator only. Links use plain
HTTP and carry only public data (the draft, the cards, and the sealed file), so
they do not replace the call: compare the chain fingerprint and every key id
before anyone starts.

#### 3. Each operator makes a key and a member card

On your own machine:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain request supply.draft.yaml
```

It asks for your operator name and the address other members reach your node
at: a host name or IP, and two ports (defaults: node-to-node `13337`, HTTP
`8080`). On a devnet where everyone is on one machine, the host is
`127.0.0.1` and each operator needs different ports. For scripts, pass
`--name`, `--host`, `--node-port`, `--http-port`, and `--yes`.

> **✓ You should see**
>
> ```text
> ✓ Created node directory …/yano-node with a new member key (keep it safe; it never leaves this directory)
> ✓ Wrote ./alice.member  (key id a6622032b8e615ee, reachable at 127.0.0.1:13337)
> ```

Your private key is now in `yano-node/secrets/member.key`, readable only by
you. Never send it. Send `alice.member` to the coordinator, and note your
**key id**: you read it out on the call.

#### 4. The coordinator seals the application

Put every card next to the draft. To see who is still missing:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain status supply.draft.yaml
```

When every card is there, seal:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain seal supply.draft.yaml
```

> **✓ You should see**
>
> ```text
> ✓ Sealed .../supply.chain
> Application supply on devnet (Yano 0.1.0-pre18, Yano X 0.1.0-pre4)
>   3 members, 2 signatures per block, governed membership
>   alice        key a6622032b8e615ee  127.0.0.1:14437  (lead)
>   bob          key 9be1fb9123767845  127.0.0.1:14438
>   carol        key 3a8ffa66e7726d76  127.0.0.1:14439
>   chain orders         audit-log              genesis 6997e41df21f3339…
>   chain fingerprint 94c9-2bad-1c59-cc7c-5e76-efed-e968-ab2e
> ```

`seal` refuses a card for a different invite, a card with a bad signature, an
unexpected name, or a key used twice. It fixes every chain's settings, the
release versions, and the digests of the plugin bundles in this distribution.
Send `supply.chain` to every operator.

`seal` also checks what a chain can do from its first block:

- An authenticated-map collection that uses a schema must set
  `valueEncoding: canonical-cbor`; otherwise `seal` refuses.
- A governed or approval collection without an active policy at genesis is
  sealed with a warning: it accepts no writes until the governance authority
  activates a policy.
- A `role-approvals` or `role-evidence` chain starts with no organizations or
  actors. `seal` writes a template plan beside the sealed file, for example
  `approvals.role-plan.yaml`, and prints the next step: fill it in and, once
  the application is live, run
  `./yano.sh appchain role bootstrap --plan approvals.role-plan.yaml`. See
  [role approvals](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/role-approvals/).

#### 5. Compare the fingerprint, then join

Hold a short call. The coordinator reads out the **chain fingerprint**; each
operator reads out their own **key id** and checks it is listed under their
name. A card proves a key, not who sent it, so this call is the trust step.

Then each operator joins:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain join supply.chain
```

`join` shows the same summary and asks whether the fingerprint and every key
id match. In a script, pass the fingerprint you compared instead:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain join supply.chain \
  --expect-fingerprint 94c9-2bad-1c59-cc7c-5e76-efed-e968-ab2e --yes
```

> **✓ You should see** `✓ Joined supply (94c9-2bad-…) in …/yano-node`, then
> `Next: yano.sh appchain start`.

`join` refuses if your key is not in the roster under your name, if the file
does not match the fingerprint, or if your plugin bundles differ from the
sealed ones. It writes the node configuration from the sealed settings; it
never works them out again, so every operator runs exactly the same chain. On
Linux it also writes a systemd unit; see
[Run your node on a server](https://yano-x.io/deployment/operators/).

#### 6. Start, and check the status

Each operator starts their node:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain start
```

On a devnet the **lead starts first**: its node creates the Cardano devnet,
and the other nodes download that genesis from it on their first start. On
preview, preprod, or mainnet every node syncs Cardano itself first, which can
take a while; watch `yano-node/logs/node.log`.

> **✓ You should see** `✓ Node alice is up at http://127.0.0.1:8080`.

Then check the whole application from any member:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain status supply
```

> **✓ You should see**
>
> ```text
> supply  chain fingerprint 94c9-2bad-1c59-cc7c-5e76-efed-e968-ab2e
>   Draft ─ Members ─ Sealed ─ Starting ─ [Live]
>   members online 3/3
>     alice        key a6622032b8e615ee  online   http://127.0.0.1:9180
>     bob          key 9be1fb9123767845  online   http://127.0.0.1:9181
>     carol        key 3a8ffa66e7726d76  online   http://127.0.0.1:9182
>   chain orders         height 0      members agree  members 3, 2 signatures  anchoring: not set up
>   Cardano: devnet block 1834, genesis 5b0e9f6c2a41d7e3 (compare with the other members)
>   Plugins: catalog sha256:4f1a2c9be07d5a31… (compare with the other members)
> ```

Until everyone is up, the stage is `Starting` and `Next:` names who to ask.
For scripts, `status --json` prints the same view, and
`status supply --wait live --timeout 600` waits until the application is live.

The last two lines describe your own node, and every member compares them:

- **Cardano** on preview, preprod, or mainnet shows the latest block and
  `up to date`, or `syncing: about 3 hours behind` while the node catches up.
  On a devnet it shows the hash of the devnet genesis this node stored; every
  member must show the same one.
- **Plugins** is the fingerprint of the plugin catalog this node loaded. A
  different value on one member means it runs different plugins, so that
  member cannot agree on blocks; install the release the application was
  sealed with.

#### 7. Send a message and see it final

Your node's API key is in `yano-node/secrets/api.key`. Read it into your shell
without printing it, and submit through your own node (use your HTTP port):

```bash
API_KEY=$(cat yano-node/secrets/api.key)
MESSAGE_ID=$(curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/app-chain/chains/orders/messages \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"topic":"orders","body":"order A-100 created"}' | jq -er .messageId)
echo "Accepted message $MESSAGE_ID"
```

A successful submission means "accepted", not "final". A few seconds later,
look it up:

```bash
curl -fsS -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/app-chain/chains/orders/messages/$MESSAGE_ID" | jq .height
```

> **✓ You should see** a height of 1 or more. Until the message is final, the
> lookup answers 404.

Run `status supply` again: every member shows the same height and
`members agree`. Follow [the proof guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/docs/appchain/PROOF_LAB.md) to retrieve and
verify a proof for the message.

#### 8. Stop and start

```bash
./yano.sh appchain stop
./yano.sh appchain start
```

`stop` keeps all data. Nothing in this tool deletes chain data.

#### Optional: anchor a chain to Cardano

A chain goes live without anchoring. To write a chain's height and state root
to Cardano, one operator runs:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain anchor supply
```

It creates an anchor wallet key on that node only, shows its address and the
cost per anchor, waits for funds, and restarts the node with anchoring on. On
a devnet only the **lead** can anchor, and the lead's devnet funds the wallet.
On a public network, fund the wallet only with what you are willing to spend
on fees: its balance is the spending limit. Afterwards `status` shows the
chain's anchoring as, for example, `led by alice, 12 anchored (last height
118)`. See [anchors and verification](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/07-anchors-and-verification/).

#### Optional: protect topics

On a chain sealed with `topics:`, namespaces are created and changed with
plans. Make one from your node directory, which supplies the node, its key and
the chain:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain topics init games/     # writes topics.yaml: fill in the owner keys and policy
./yano.sh appchain topics plan topics.yaml
```

`plan` writes `topics.plan.json` and says who must act. A top-level namespace
is a member vote: send the plan to every operator, and each runs

```bash
./yano.sh appchain topics approve topics.plan.json
```

which shows what it votes for, asks for a yes (`--yes` in scripts), votes
through their own node and waits until the namespace is in effect; it never
votes twice, so it is safe to run again (`--again` votes again after an
earlier vote lapsed). On an idle chain add `--heartbeat`. Changes inside a
namespace are signed by its owners
instead: each owner runs `topics sign topics.plan.json --key-file <seed file>`,
and anyone runs `topics submit topics.signed.json`, which waits until it is in
effect. `topics public-key <seed file>` prints the public key to put in
`topics.yaml`. Studio's **Topics** page
writes `topics.yaml` with a form if you prefer. See
[protect a topic and give users session keys](https://yano-x.io/recipes/topic-session-keys/).

#### Where each setting lives

<!-- illustration: config-layers -->

Your node directory (`./yano-node` by default; change it with `--node-dir`)
holds everything for your node:

| Path | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `node.json` | Your name, public key, advertised addresses, and ports |
| `secrets/member.key`, `secrets/api.key` | Your private member key and API key; `secrets/anchor.key` only on an anchor leader |
| `apps/supply.chain` | The sealed file you joined |
| `topic-votes/`, `topic-submissions/` | The topic votes this node cast and the signed changes it submitted, so `topics approve` never votes twice and a repeated `topics submit` follows the first one |
| `config/consensus.yaml`, `config/node.yaml` | Generated by `join`; do not edit, run `join` again instead |
| `config/local.yaml` | Your own node-only settings, such as connector endpoints. `join` creates it empty and never rewrites it; its values win over `config/node.yaml`. `start` refuses it if it sets any sealed consensus setting |
| `data/` | Chain data: `chainstate`, `appchain-chainstate`, `history` |
| `logs/node.log` | The node's log |

Back up the node directory. It holds your key and your chain data.

Put settings that belong to your node alone, such as a connector's endpoint
or a log level, in `config/local.yaml`. Every member must run the sealed
values, so `start` refuses a local file that sets a key from
`config/consensus.yaml`; to change a sealed setting, seal a new application.
Keep secrets out of it: reference them through the environment.

#### Troubleshooting

| You see | What it means and what to do |
|---|---|
| `Members 2/3: waiting for carol` from `seal` | A card is missing. Ask carol to run `request` and send the card; put it next to the draft. |
| `carol.member was made for a different invite (…)` | The card was made for an older draft. Ask carol to run `request` again with the current draft. |
| `This node's key (…) is not a member of supply` | The sealed file holds someone else's card under your name. Do not start. Tell the coordinator. |
| `The fingerprint is …, not …. Do not start: the file differs from the one the coordinator sealed.` | Your `supply.chain` is not the one compared on the call. Get the file again. |
| `This distribution's plugin bundles differ from the sealed ones: …` | Install the Yano X release named in the message, the same one the coordinator sealed with. |
| `Port 8080 is already in use by another program.` | Stop that program, or make a new node directory with other ports (`request --http-port`, `--node-port`). |
| `status` stays at `Starting` with `ask the lead (alice) to run  yano.sh appchain start  first` | On a devnet the other nodes wait for the lead's devnet. Ask the lead to start. |
| `config/local.yaml changes sealed consensus settings: …` from `start` | Your local file overrides a value every member must share. Remove the named keys from `config/local.yaml`. |
| `Port 7099 is in use; pass --port with a free one` from `invite --serve` | Choose another port with `--port`; the links printed afterwards carry it. |
| `The links expired before every operator received the sealed file` | Run `invite --serve` again; it prints new links. Operators who already sent a card can rerun `request` with their new link. |
| `Plugins:` differs between members | That member loads different plugins. Install the Yano X release the application was sealed with. |
| The devnet genesis in `Cardano:` differs between members | That node follows a different devnet from the lead's. Stop it and tell the coordinator before it signs anything. |

**Next:** [grow and change the application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/add-chain/), or
[run your node on a server](https://yano-x.io/deployment/operators/).

---

## Optional first-party connectors

Source: https://yano-x.io/deployment/connectors/

> Kafka, S3-compatible storage, IPFS/Kubo, and Cardano payments are maintained Yano integrations, but they are not present in the stock distribution. They…

Kafka, S3-compatible storage, IPFS/Kubo, and Cardano payments are maintained
Yano integrations, but they are not present in the stock distribution. They
are `FIRST_PARTY_OPTIONAL`: selecting their capability creates an artifact and
configuration requirement; it does not install a plugin or provision an
external service.

#### Packaging matrix

| Integration | Capabilities | JVM bundle task | External ownership |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kafka | `executor:kafka`, `sink:kafka` | `:connectors:kafka:shadowJar` | Brokers, TLS/SASL identity, credentials, topic ACLs and retention |
| S3-compatible object storage | `executor:objectstore-s3` | `:connectors:objectstore-s3:shadowJar` | Versioned buckets, create-only policy, credentials, encryption and retention |
| IPFS/Kubo | `executor:ipfs` | `:connectors:ipfs:shadowJar` | Kubo API identity, authentication, pin durability and replication |
| Cardano payments | `executor:cardano-payment` | `:connectors:effects-cardano:shadowJar` | Funded payer, signing-key custody, backend trust, caps and reconciliation |

Build one JVM plugin from the repository root, for example:

```bash
./gradlew :connectors:kafka:shadowJar
```

Copy only the resulting `*-bundle.jar` into the plugin directory of every node
that owns that sink or executor. The default directory is `plugins/`; an
operator may override it with `yano.plugins.directory`. Keep the plugin version
aligned with the Yano release:

```bash
cp connectors/kafka/build/libs/*-bundle.jar /opt/yano/plugins/
```

A node set up with `appchain join` checks only the bundles its chains were
sealed with at every `appchain start`; adding a connector bundle does not change
them. Replacing one of those sealed bundles does, and `start` then refuses until
the operator accepts the new set with `appchain join <app>.chain --accept-bundles`.

Do not copy a thin build-time JAR into the JVM plugin directory. These connector
bundles are JVM-only and cannot be installed beside Yano's native executable.

#### Configuration boundary

Consensus records contain a stable effect type, target alias, and bounded
action payload. Endpoints, credentials, wallet keys, TLS material, bucket
names, and broker/Kubo/backend policy are node-local. Never put them into an
effect payload, setup draft, sealed `.chain` file, or shared consensus YAML.

On a node set up with `appchain join`, put a connector's node-local settings
in `config/local.yaml` in the node directory. `join` creates that file and
never rewrites it, and its values win over the generated `config/node.yaml`.
`start` refuses it if it sets any sealed consensus setting. Supply credentials
through the environment or a secret provider, not in the file itself.

At-least-once execution is intentional. Targets must use the effect ID as an
idempotency key or provide the connector's documented reconciliation
semantics. An accepted effect is not proof that the external system acted;
verify the incorporated result and the external receipt.

#### Kafka

Kafka contributes two independent features:

- `sink:kafka` publishes finalized app blocks; and
- `executor:kafka` executes allowlisted `kafka.publish` effects.

The sink and executor have separate configuration. Both require a node-local
security profile and operator-owned topic policy. See the
[Kafka integration guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/connectors/kafka/README.md).

#### S3-compatible object storage

The `object.put` executor promotes a pre-staged, hash-verified object into a
versioned immutable destination. The target configuration owns endpoints,
buckets, credentials, encryption and retention. Its create-only bucket-policy
and version-history requirements are part of correctness, not optional
hardening. See the
[object-store guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/connectors/objectstore-s3/README.md).

#### IPFS/Kubo

The `ipfs.pin` executor pins an already known CID. It does not add document
bytes, derive a CID, expose a gateway, or promise permanent replication. See
the [IPFS guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/connectors/ipfs/README.md).

#### Cardano payments

The `cardano.payment` executor controls material funds and therefore has a
stricter readiness boundary. Use an operator-controlled payer, explicit
network/backend, transaction cap, protected signing credential, and a funded
testnet rehearsal before production. See the
[Cardano effects guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/connectors/effects-cardano/README.md).

#### Release and demo distinction

The evidence demo stages Kafka, S3 and IPFS plugins and local services to prove
the complete scenario. That does not make those plugins bundled in the normal
Yano distribution. Always use the release capability catalog
(`./yano.sh appchain capabilities`) and the bundles in the distribution's
`plugins/` directory, not the contents of a demo Compose environment, as
packaging truth.

---

## Run your node on a server

Source: https://yano-x.io/deployment/operators/

> Your node runs as a systemd service, and status shows every member online.

- **Goal:** run your member node on your own Linux server, as a service that
  survives reboots, reachable by the other members.
- **Before you start:** a Linux VM with systemd, `sudo`, Java 25, and the same
  extracted Yano X JVM release the coordinator used. The cloud showcase route
  at the end also needs OpenTofu and Ansible.
- **Outcome:** your node runs as a systemd service, and `status` shows every
  member online.

Each operator deploys their own node. There is no cluster-wide export: the
coordinator never touches your server, and your private key never leaves it.
The steps are the same as in [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/); this page
covers what changes on a server.

#### 1. Make your card with your public address

On your server, from the extracted Yano X directory:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain request supply.draft.yaml --host node-a.example.com
```

Use the host name or IP the **other members** reach your server at, not
`127.0.0.1`. With a public host, the node listens on all interfaces. The
default ports are node-to-node `13337` and HTTP `8080`; choose others with
`--node-port` and `--http-port`. If a NAT or proxy forwards a different port
to your server, keep the advertised one in the card and later run
`join --listen <port>` with the local one.

> **✓ You should see** `✓ Wrote ./alice.member  (key id …, reachable at
> node-a.example.com:13337)`.

If the coordinator sent you a join link instead of the draft, give the link
in place of the file, with the same options:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain request 'yano://coord.example.com:7099/…#…' --host node-a.example.com
```

It sends your card, waits for the seal, saves `supply.chain`, and continues
into `join` (step 3). On a server without a terminal session to keep open,
add `--no-wait` and run the same command again later to collect the sealed
file. See [join links](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/#easier-hand-out-join-links).

#### 2. Open the ports

| Port | Who needs it | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Node-to-node, `13337` | The other members' servers | Blocks, votes, and catch-up |
| HTTP, `8080` | The other operators, and your own applications | `status` reads each member's chain status from it; on a devnet the other nodes download the devnet genesis from the lead's |
| Join links, `7099` | The operators, only while the coordinator runs `invite --serve` | Hands out the draft, collects the cards, and hands out the sealed file. Only the coordinator's machine needs it, and only during setup |

Open them only to the machines that need them. Write calls on the HTTP API
need your API key (`yano-node/secrets/api.key`); put TLS and a reverse proxy
in front before any client outside your network uses it. On a devnet the
lead's HTTP port also serves the devnet's unauthenticated time and rollback
controls, so keep a shared devnet on a trusted network.

#### 3. Join and install the service

When the coordinator sends `supply.chain` and you have compared the
fingerprint on the call:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain join supply.chain
```

On Linux, `join` also writes a systemd unit into your node directory and
prints the command to install it:

> **✓ You should see**
>
> ```text
> ✓ Joined supply (94c9-2bad-…) in /home/alice/yano-x-jvm-<version>/yano-node
>   To run it as a service: sudo cp …/yano-node/yano-appchain-alice.service /etc/systemd/system/ && sudo systemctl enable --now yano-appchain-alice.service
> ```

Run that command. The tool never installs the unit itself. The service runs
as the user who ran `join`, and restarts the node if it fails.

Once the unit is installed and enabled, `./yano.sh appchain start` and
`stop`, and the restarts that `approve` and `anchor` make, go through
`systemctl`, so one node never has two managers. You can also use systemd
directly:

```bash
systemctl status yano-appchain-alice.service
journalctl -u yano-appchain-alice.service
```

On a devnet the lead starts first. On a public network the node syncs Cardano
before its chains make progress; the `Cardano:` line of `status` shows
`syncing: about N hours behind` until it reports `up to date`, and
`yano-node/logs/node.log` has the details.

#### Node-only settings

`config/consensus.yaml` and `config/node.yaml` are rewritten by `join`. Put
anything that belongs to your node alone, such as connector endpoints for an
effect executor, in `config/local.yaml` in the node directory. `join` creates
it, never rewrites it, and its values win over `config/node.yaml`. `start`
refuses the file if it sets any sealed consensus setting, because every member
must run the sealed values. Keep credentials in the environment or a secret
provider rather than in the file. See
[optional connectors](https://yano-x.io/deployment/connectors/).

#### 4. Check the application

```bash
./yano.sh appchain status supply
```

> **✓ You should see** `[Live]`, every member `online`, and `members agree`
> for every chain. An `offline` member is named, with the address `status`
> tried. Compare the `Plugins:` catalog fingerprint (and, on a devnet, the
> genesis in `Cardano:`) with the other operators: they must match.

#### What to back up and monitor

- **Back up** the whole node directory: `secrets/` holds your member key, and
  `data/` holds the authoritative stores `chainstate` and
  `appchain-chainstate`. Do not copy an open RocksDB directory as a backup;
  stop the node first. With fixed sequencing the lead's key cannot be
  replaced.
- **Monitor** `status` (members online, heights, agreement, anchoring,
  Cardano sync), the node log, disk space, and process health. If fewer members than the
  threshold are online, the chains stop finalizing until enough return; that
  is the safety the threshold buys. With fixed sequencing, if the lead is
  offline the others still finalize through a certified view change, but each
  block first waits for a round timeout, so watch the lead.

#### Showcase on cloud VMs

The packaged `tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy` deploys the curated
showcase profile, not your own application, to existing Linux VMs, Contabo,
Hetzner Cloud, DigitalOcean, or mixed placement. It generates OpenTofu and
Ansible inputs, configures systemd and storage, and checks readiness before
opening ingress. From the extracted JVM release:

```bash
tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy init ./vm-cluster --nodes 3
### Edit vm-cluster/deployment.yaml: actual hosts, placement, network, and secret references.
### Complete the profile's settlement deployment record and bootstrap prerequisites.
tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy artifact import ./vm-cluster \
  --file /path/to/yano-x-jvm-<version>.zip
tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy validate ./vm-cluster
tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy doctor ./vm-cluster
tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy plan ./vm-cluster
```

> **✓ You should see** `Imported showcase archive sha256:...` after the import.
> The import refuses an archive without `yano.sh`, `yano.jar`, and the
> `examples/showcase/` profile.

Read the [full operator runbook](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/deployment/README.md) for SSH bootstrap,
provider credentials, OS and capacity checks, network policy, and manifest fields.
The current profile requires Preprod anchoring and settlement configuration.
Public addresses in generated examples are documentation placeholders.

Apply only to the intended reviewed cluster:

```bash
tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy apply ./vm-cluster --confirm <cluster-id>
tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy status ./vm-cluster
tools/yano-deploy/bin/yano-x-deploy wait ./vm-cluster --for l1-tip --timeout-seconds 3600
```

Apply can cause a full-cluster interruption for mesh recovery with the pinned
host. It is not a zero-downtime rolling upgrade. Anchoring and settlement
bootstrap are separate operations; authorize public-network transactions explicitly.

**Next:** [from demonstration to production](https://yano-x.io/deployment/production/).

---

## From demonstration to production

Source: https://yano-x.io/deployment/production/

> Every recipe, showcase chain, and product in this repository ships with a launcher, demo actors, and fixed local keys, and every one of those is a…

Every recipe, showcase chain, and product in this repository ships with a launcher, demo actors,
and fixed local keys, and every one of those is a demonstration convenience. This guide says what
changes when a consortium runs an app ledger for real: how the genesis is agreed, where keys live,
what each service is allowed to reach, and which parts are still gated.

Yano is pre-release. Nothing here makes a `preview` or `EXPERIMENTAL` component production-ready on
its own; read its status first.

#### The short version

| Demo | Production |
|---|---|
| Seeds derived from a public string | Keys generated by each actor, on their own machine, never transmitted |
| One process holding every seed | One signer per organization, holding only its own key |
| A fixed local API key | A per-caller key, rotated, never in a shell history or a repository |
| Loopback HTTP, no TLS | TLS on every reachable endpoint, with a reverse proxy in front |
| Members and threshold chosen by a script | Members agreed by the consortium in the draft, sealed, and checked by fingerprint |
| Anchoring to a self-contained devnet | Anchoring to preprod or mainnet from a funded, protected key |
| One operator playing every role | Each organization operating its own node and signer |

#### 1. Agree the genesis

The genesis fixes the collections, the schemas, the roles, the policies, and the actors with their
public keys. Its hash is the genesis id, and every authorization is signed against it, so agreeing
it is the first governance act and changing it later means a different ledger.

**Each actor generates its own key.** On the actor's own machine, never on the operator's, the
actor derives its public key and signs a chain-bound proof of possession:

```bash
PUBLIC_KEY="$(./yano.sh appchain role public-key --seed-file <seed>)"
./yano.sh appchain role key-proof-signature --chain <chain-id> --actor <actor-id> \
  --actor-revision 1 --key <key-id> --public-key "$PUBLIC_KEY" \
  --valid-from-height 1 --valid-until-height 0 --seed-file <seed>
```

The public key and the proof travel to the operator. The seed does not: it stays in a file readable
only by its owner, or in a key store or HSM the organization already trusts.

**The coordinator writes the genesis** for a governed authenticated map: the collections, policies,
organizations, actors, public keys and proofs the consortium agreed go into the chain's
`authenticatedMap` entry in the application draft, and `./yano.sh appchain seal` fixes the chain
configuration and its genesis id (see [governed collections](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/authenticated-map/#governed-collections)
and [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/)). Actors added after genesis go through
[role approvals](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/role-approvals/), whose `appchain role bootstrap` encodes the
propose, approve and activate commands, with proofs from `appchain role key-proof`.

**Every member checks the sealed file before joining.** On a call, the coordinator reads out the
chain fingerprint, which covers every chain's settings and genesis id, the members, the threshold,
and the plugin bundle digests; each operator reads out its own key id. `join` shows the same summary,
recomputes a derived genesis id, and refuses a node whose own key is not in the roster. A
participant whose fingerprint differs should not join the ledger. Publish the fingerprint and the
genesis ids where members and verifiers can check them.

Note what cannot be changed afterwards without a new ledger: the collections, their policies, the
actors declared at genesis, the block interval, and the message size bounds. Adding an actor later
is a governance action on the role workflow.

#### 2. Members, threshold, and nodes

The member set is the list of node keys whose signatures certify a block, and the threshold is how
many must sign. Both are consortium decisions, not defaults, and every verifier must pin the same set.

Size the threshold against two separate risks. Up to `n − t` members can be offline while the ledger
keeps finalizing blocks. Dishonest members are a separate assumption: the fault bound `f`, set as
`consensus.max-byzantine-members`, is 0 by default, and the node refuses to start unless
`2t − n > f` and `t ≤ n − f`. A threshold of two of three therefore tolerates one member being down,
but not one dishonest member: it cannot be configured with `f = 1`. Tolerating one dishonest member
takes, for example, four members with a threshold of three and `f = 1`.

Each organization runs its own node, with its own storage, and its own signing key. Do not run a
"cluster" of nodes owned by one operator and call it a consortium: the threshold then proves only
that one operator signed several times. The showcase launcher does exactly that, which is why it is
a demonstration.

Each organization sets up its node with `./yano.sh appchain request` and `join`, and runs it with
`start` (see [Run your node on a server](https://yano-x.io/deployment/operators/)). `join` writes the sealed settings
as they are, including the block interval and message size bounds that are part of the genesis
identity, so every node runs exactly the same chain. Members are added and removed later with
`./yano.sh appchain approve` ([Grow and change](https://yano-x.io/deployment/add-chain/)).

Each node keeps its own node directory. Back up its key and its authoritative stores, `chainstate/` and
`appchain-chainstate/` (see [where data lives](https://yano-x.io/concepts/where-data-lives/)), and decide a
retention policy for proofs and history before you need one. Historical answers need proof retention: a verifier asking
about height H needs the node to still hold it.

#### 3. Keys and signing

This is where a demonstration differs most from a deployment.

**Do not run a shared signer in production.** A service that signs for every actor whose seed it
was started with lets whoever reaches it write as any of them. In a demo that is the point; in a
deployment it collapses the distinction the ledger is there to make. Each organization signs only
for its own actors, on its own machine, reachable only by its own operators. Hardware and
wallet-held keys are not implemented yet.

**API keys** authenticate callers to the node, and are not identities. Issue one per caller, keep
them out of shell history and repositories, and rotate them.

**Authorization lifetimes** are bounded in blocks and one-use. A signer that is offline long enough
for its authorization to expire simply retries; do not raise the lifetime to avoid that.

#### 4. Network and services

Everything binds to loopback by default. That default is correct, and exposing a service is a
deliberate act:

| Service | Exposure | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Node REST API | private to the operators and services that need it | never public; put TLS and a reverse proxy in front |
| Your application's read service | public, read only, if it serves proofs | no secret, no write route |
| A signer | private to one organization's operators | holds keys; never public, and never without TLS if it leaves the host |
| Static UIs | static files | can be public; they hold no secret beyond what the operator types |

A UI served over HTTPS cannot call a service over plain HTTP. Either serve both over HTTPS, or host
the UI behind the same reverse proxy as the service so they share an origin.

#### 5. Anchoring to Cardano

The demo anchors to a devnet the cluster runs itself. In production, anchoring is what turns
"the consortium says so" into "a public chain carries it".

- Choose the network deliberately, and confirm public anchoring explicitly. Preprod for testing;
  mainnet only when the operator accepts the cost and the permanence.
- Anchoring needs a funded wallet key. Keep it in a file the launcher reads, owner-only, outside
  the data directory, and treat it as a production secret. Never pass a seed on a command line.
- Only some ledgers need anchoring. Anchor the ones whose evidence must be independently checkable
  later, and leave the rest.
- Verifiers reach the top trust level by reading the anchor datum from a Cardano source they trust
  and verifying against the block it commits to. Plan how your verifiers get that datum: a public
  resolver, a block explorer, or their own node.
- Nothing public should carry personal data. On-chain metadata and datums are permanent.

#### 6. What the demo does that production must not

- Derive seeds from a public string. Every demo actor's key is computable by anyone.
- Use the known local API key, or leave one in an environment printed by a launcher.
- Run one signer holding every organization's key.
- Run all members from one operator, one host, and one directory.
- Bind services to a public interface without TLS.
- Treat a `preview` or `EXPERIMENTAL` component as a supported one.

#### 7. Per-product notes

- **Evidence** publishes to object storage, IPFS, and Kafka through connectors. Give each connector
  its own credentials, and treat the effect secrets as production secrets.
- **Cardano History** answers from the L1 data its node observed. Proofs are pinned to the latest
  L1-confirmed commitment, so its chain must be anchored.
- **The eUTxO ledger** is experimental and for disposable test funds only.

#### 8. Before you go live

- Every member compared the chain fingerprint and its own key id before joining.
- Each organization holds its own signing key, and no key is on a machine that did not generate it.
- The member set and threshold are recorded where verifiers can obtain them.
- TLS terminates in front of every reachable endpoint, and the node API is not among them.
- Anchoring, if used, has a funded key that is backed up and access-controlled.
- Retention is decided, backups are tested, and a member can be restored.
- Every verifier knows which trust level they require.
- Each component's classification and its deferred stages are written down where the operator's
  stakeholders can read them.

---

## Composite profile governance

Source: https://yano-x.io/deployment/profile-governance/

> This runbook is for operators evolving the deterministic composite state machine of a long-lived app ledger. The short rule is:

This runbook is for operators evolving the deterministic composite state machine
of a long-lived app ledger. The short rule is:

> Deploy the dormant target code everywhere first; authorize one exact profile
> and activation height on the ledger second.

Profile governance changes deterministic application composition. It is not a
plugin hot-reload mechanism and it does not dynamically assemble components
from YAML. A reviewed composite bundle owns a bounded catalog of executable
profiles. Governance can select only an exact canonical profile already in that
catalog.

#### The lifecycle

A proposal moves through three statuses, `STAGING`, `SEALED`, and `SCHEDULED`.
Activation and voiding are events: when either happens, the proposal record is
deleted. Only one proposal can be open at a time.

<!-- illustration: profile-governance -->
1. **Deploy the target bundle.** Every member deploys the same bundle, whose
   catalog holds the active profile and the dormant target profile.
2. **Begin.** The author submits `BEGIN` with the active profile's digest, the
   membership digest, the target digest, the activation height `H`, and an
   expiry. The proposal is `STAGING`.
3. **Stage the chunks.** The author stages the target profile's canonical
   bytes, chunk by chunk.
4. **Seal.** The author seals the proposal; the staged bytes and the transition
   are checked, and the proposal is `SEALED` with a proposal hash.
5. **Approve.** A threshold of members approves the proposal hash.
6. **Attest readiness.** Every member attests that the target digest is in its
   local executable catalog.
7. **Scheduled.** With threshold approvals and readiness from every member
   before `H`, the proposal is `SCHEDULED`.
8. **Activate at H.** Block `H` runs the target profile; a new profile epoch is
   recorded and the proposal is deleted.
<!-- /illustration -->

#### Start a governed chain

Governed mode is a consensus-affecting choice for a new chain:

```properties
yano.app-chain.chains[0].state-machine=composite
yano.app-chain.chains[0].machines.composite.preset=evidence-v1-gated
yano.app-chain.chains[0].membership.mode=governed
yano.app-chain.chains[0].machines.composite.profile-mode=governed
yano.app-chain.chains[0].machines.composite.profile-governance.min-activation-lag=20
yano.app-chain.chains[0].machines.composite.profile-governance.proposal-ttl-blocks=600
yano.app-chain.chains[0].machines.composite.profile-governance.max-epochs=1024
```

Do not turn a retained `fixed` chain into `governed` by editing this setting.
The authenticated governance configuration and epoch-0 marker make that fail
closed. Start a new chain or, while Yano remains preview and history is
disposable, reset that chain's app-state on every member.

The stock bundle currently contains one executable preset per selected stock
composition. It exercises governed genesis, proofs, status, packaging, and
operations, but it cannot authorize a profile that is not in its catalog. A
domain bundle enables real evolution by packaging the current and dormant
target `CompositeProfileCatalog.Entry` values together.

One v1 bundle may contain 1-64 distinct canonical profiles. `max-epochs` bounds
the total authenticated epoch history, including transitions back to an already
packaged profile; it does not raise that 64-profile catalog bound. Keep every
historical profile in the catalog. V1 has no authenticated replay floor that
would make removing old executable code safe.

#### Prepare the target bundle

Before proposing anything:

1. Build a composite provider whose catalog contains both the active profile
   and the target profile, including every component/workflow generation
   present in retained epoch history or needed for late effect results.
2. Run replay, restart, snapshot, effect-result, quota-drain, and profile
   golden-vector tests for that catalog.
3. Export the exact `CompositeProfile.canonicalBytes()` for the target as a
   binary review artifact. Its domain-separated digest is the proposal target.
4. Deploy the same manifested bundle to every JVM member.
5. Rolling-restart one member at a time. A member without the target may keep
   following the old profile, but it cannot honestly attest readiness.

Plugin JARs are deployed through the documented JVM plugin-directory flow.
Yano X does not publish a native composite extension.

#### Inspect and encode commands

The distribution includes a dependency-free operator helper,
`tools/composite-profile/profile-governance.py`. It encodes each governance
command as canonical CBOR. Run it from the distribution's top-level directory:

```bash
./tools/composite-profile/profile-governance.py --chain evidence-chain begin --encode-only \
  --proposal-id "$PROPOSAL_ID" \
  --base-digest "$ACTIVE_PROFILE_DIGEST" \
  --membership-digest "$MEMBERSHIP_EPOCH_DIGEST" \
  --profile target-profile.cbor \
  --activation-height 1200 --expiry-height 1500 > begin.json
```

The output contains `targetProfileDigest`, `chunkCount`, `proposalHash`, and
`bodyHex`. Read the active profile digest and `currentMembershipDigest` from the
chain status. Always verify that the same membership epoch remains effective
through the planned activation height.

> **Known issue.** The helper's online mode, which runs without
> `--encode-only` (`status`, submit, and `--dry-run`), calls
> `/api/v1/app-chain/chains/{chain}/profile-governance` routes that the node
> does not serve. Use `--encode-only`, then send the encoded bytes to the
> composite plugin's route, as shown below.

The composite plugin serves governance under
`/api/v1/plugins/org.yanoproject.x.composite/chains/{chain}/profile-governance`:
a `GET` returns the governance status as CBOR, and a `POST` to `…/commands`
takes one command as a raw CBOR body. The `POST` is a privileged route, so it
needs the member's full API key, and `?dry-run=true` runs local validation
without submitting. The member's own node submits the command with its member
key:

```bash
NODE=https://member-a.example:7070
ROUTE=/api/v1/plugins/org.yanoproject.x.composite/chains/evidence-chain/profile-governance/commands

### Once: an owner-only header file. printf is a shell builtin and cat is given
### only the file name, so the key never appears in a process's arguments.
(umask 077; { printf 'X-API-Key: '; cat /secure/member-a.key; } > /secure/member-a.headers)

jq -r .bodyHex begin.json | xxd -r -p > begin.cbor
curl -sS -X POST -H @/secure/member-a.headers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' --data-binary @begin.cbor \
  "$NODE$ROUTE?dry-run=true"          # {"validated":true}
curl -sS -X POST -H @/secure/member-a.headers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' --data-binary @begin.cbor \
  "$NODE$ROUTE"                       # {"messageId":"…"}
```

`-H @file` (curl 7.55 or later) reads the header from the file, so curl's
arguments name only the file. Never put the key itself in a command, where
other users and monitoring agents can read the process arguments, or in shell
history. Keep both files owner-only. Use HTTPS for every non-loopback member
endpoint and terminate it only at an operator-trusted proxy.

Stage each reported chunk and seal the proposal, waiting for each command to
finalize before the next step:

```bash
./tools/composite-profile/profile-governance.py --chain evidence-chain chunk --encode-only \
  --proposal-id "$PROPOSAL_ID" --profile target-profile.cbor --index 0

./tools/composite-profile/profile-governance.py --chain evidence-chain seal --encode-only \
  --proposal-id "$PROPOSAL_ID"
```

Repeat `chunk` for indices `0 .. chunkCount-1`. Conflicting or duplicate
non-identical chunks void the proposal; identical replay is a no-op.

#### Approve, attest readiness, and activate

Approval and readiness are deliberately separate:

- threshold member approvals authorize the exact intent;
- every member in the bound membership epoch must attest that the exact target
  digest exists in its local executable catalog.

Each approving member encodes its commands and submits them through its own
node, as above, so its own member key signs them:

```bash
./tools/composite-profile/profile-governance.py --chain evidence-chain approve --encode-only \
  --proposal-hash "$PROPOSAL_HASH"

./tools/composite-profile/profile-governance.py --chain evidence-chain ready --encode-only \
  --proposal-hash "$PROPOSAL_HASH" --target-digest "$TARGET_DIGEST"
```

A dry run of `READY` is the final local diagnostic. It fails when that node's
catalog lacks the target. Once the threshold and all-member readiness are
finalized, status becomes `SCHEDULED`. Every block before `H` uses the old
profile; block `H` uses the target for results, expiries, workflows, and normal
messages. There is no local break-glass override.

Cancel before activation when necessary:

```bash
./tools/composite-profile/profile-governance.py --chain evidence-chain cancel --encode-only \
  --proposal-hash "$PROPOSAL_HASH"
```

Threshold cancellations void a proposal. It is also voided by expiry, by a
change of the bound membership epoch, by malformed or conflicting staging, by a
seal whose bytes or digest do not match, by invalid profile compatibility or
quota rules, and by approvals and readiness that complete only at or after `H`.
A `BEGIN` whose base digest is not the active profile is ignored rather than
recorded.

#### Observe and verify

The chain status/UI projects the active epoch, digest, proposal state,
activation height, approvals, readiness, local readiness, and retired drains.
Prometheus exports:

- `yano.appchain.composite.profile.epoch`;
- `yano.appchain.composite.governance.proposal.state` (`0` none, `1` staging,
  `2` sealed, `3` scheduled);
- `yano.appchain.composite.governance.approvals`;
- `yano.appchain.composite.governance.readiness`;
- `yano.appchain.composite.governance.local.ready`; and
- `yano.appchain.composite.governance.retired.drains`.

Health reports `{chain}.scheduledProfileMissing=true` and goes down if a node
has a scheduled target absent from its local catalog. This is a last-resort
alarm, not permission to schedule before all members are ready.

Proof clients have two policies:

- strict clients verify an MPF proof for the active marker at a trusted
  finalized root, then pin its expected digest; and
- governance-aware clients verify finality and MPF inclusion for the current
  epoch pointer, every retained epoch record, and the active marker at the same
  root. They then check byte linkage with
  `CompositeProfileEpochChainVerifier.verifyStructure(...)` and independently
  enforce their membership/approval policy from finalized block history.

The dependency-free structural verifier does not fetch proofs or prove member
authorization; it only checks the already-proven bytes supplied by the caller.
For a complete offline trust-boundary check, use
`yano-x-composite-client`'s `GovernedCompositeVerifier`: it first verifies
portable block finality against caller-pinned membership, then verifies the
pointer, every epoch, and the marker as MPF inclusions at that exact root,
checks canonical linkage, and finally invokes the caller's mandatory
membership/approval-history policy. Applications with a fully reviewed
proposal schedule can use `requirePinnedProposalHashes(...)`; it fails unless
every non-genesis epoch has exactly the expected proposal hash, with no missing
or extra epoch. Neither policy makes unreviewed component code trustworthy.

#### Recovery rules

- Missing bundle before readiness: deploy it and retry local dry-run/`READY`.
- Membership changes before activation: the proposal is void; repropose against
  the new membership epoch.
- Missed activation after falsely claiming readiness: restore the exact bundle
  and catch up from finalized history; do not edit profile state.
- Bad profile already activated: authorize a corrected future epoch. Never
  rewrite the marker, epoch records, or local database to create a hidden fork.
- Lost governance threshold: use the membership-governance recovery policy
  first; profile governance cannot bypass membership authority.

The complete consensus contract is recorded in the repository's ADR-015.

---

## Troubleshooting

Source: https://yano-x.io/deployment/troubleshooting/

> Symptoms you are likely to meet when you run an app ledger, what causes them, and how to fix them. Commands assume an extracted yano-x-jvm-<version>.zip…

Symptoms you are likely to meet when you run an app ledger, what causes them,
and how to fix them. Commands assume an extracted `yano-x-jvm-<version>.zip`
and a node set up with the [setup commands](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/). Each
command takes the node directory as `--node-dir` (default `./yano-node`;
`./yano.sh appchain try` puts its nodes in `appchain-try/<name>/yano-node`).
The showcase wraps the same commands as `./showcase.sh <command> --instance <name>`.

Start with these two:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain status --node-dir yano-node   # members online, per-chain height, agreement, anchoring
tail -n 60 yano-node/logs/node.log               # the last lines of this node's log; tail -f follows it
```

Each node's `GET /api/v1/app-chain/chains/{chainId}/status` reports its role,
tip height, state root, pending pool size, peers, and whether it is `stalled`.

#### A port is busy

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `start` says `Port N is already in use by another program` | A node's HTTP and node ports are fixed when `request` makes its key, and another program holds one of them. | Stop whatever holds the port, or set the node up again with other ports: a new `--node-dir` and `request --http-port <port> --node-port <port>`. |
| `try` used ports other than 8080 and 13337 | `try` gives each node the first free ports from 8080 (HTTP) and 13337 (node), so it skipped ports in use. | Use the ports in the `request` commands it printed, or read one back: `jq -r .httpPort appchain-try/alice/yano-node/node.json`. |
| The showcase fails on port 7070 | The showcase always passes its ports explicitly, defaulting to 7070 and 13337. | Start the instance with free ranges, for example `--http-base 7170 --server-base 9170`. The instance remembers them. |
| `This node is already running` | The node is already up. | Use it, or `./yano.sh appchain stop --node-dir <dir>` first. |

#### Accepted, but not final yet

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `POST …/messages` returned 202, but `GET …/messages/{id}` answers 404 `No finalized message with id …` | 202 only means one member queued the message. It is final once a block containing it is. | Poll until the lookup returns a height, as in [Configure](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/), and then read the application's result. |
| It never becomes final | Too few members are connected to reach the threshold, or the leader cannot complete rounds. | Check `./yano.sh appchain status` (members online) and the logs. A round that times out moves to the next leader automatically. |
| The message disappeared | Pending messages live in memory. A message expires from the pool after its TTL (10 minutes by default), and one that no other member had received is lost if its member restarts. | Check that it was not finalized, then submit it again. |
| Final, but nothing changed | The command broke a business rule when the block ran: a deterministic no-op on every member. | Read the result, fix the cause, and submit a new message. |

#### Members disagree: MISMATCH

`./yano.sh appchain status` prints one line per chain with `members agree` or
`MISMATCH`. `MISMATCH` means the members report different genesis identities
for the chain. It also warns `members report different state roots at height N`
when two members report different roots at the same height. Members at
different heights are not compared, and members that do not answer are
skipped. In the showcase, `./showcase.sh verify all --instance <name>` waits
until every node reports the same tip height and root.

| Cause | How to tell | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A member joined a different sealed file | `MISMATCH` on the chain's line, and the warning `members report different genesis identities; one of them joined a different sealed file` | Every member must join the same sealed `.chain` file. Compare the chain fingerprint on the first line of each member's `status`. |
| No node reports the chain | The chain is in the configuration file but not hosted, or no node is ready yet | See "A chain is missing" below. |
| A member computes a different root | Its log shows `Proposal state-root mismatch at height … — rejecting`; the member stops voting and stalls | The state machine is not deterministic, or members run different code or configuration. Compare each member's `pluginCatalogFingerprint` from its chain `identity` endpoint; for an application set up with the setup CLI, `./yano.sh appchain status <app>` also flags a member with a different genesis identity, and its `Plugins:` line shows this node's catalog fingerprint for the members to compare. See [Determinism rules](https://yano-x.io/concepts/determinism-rules/). |

#### A chain is missing

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `404 {"error":"Unknown app chain: <chainId>"}` | The node does not host that chain id. | Check the spelling: `./yano.sh appchain status` lists the chains of the application this node joined. To add one, follow [Add a chain](https://yano-x.io/deployment/add-chain/). |
| `400 … app chains are hosted — use /app-chain/chains/{chainId}/...` | A route without a chain id was used on a node that hosts several chains. | Use the chain-scoped route `/api/v1/app-chain/chains/{chainId}/…`. |
| `503 App chain is not enabled on this node` | The node hosts no app ledger. | Add a chain to the node's configuration. |
| The node does not start: `… is not in the configured member list (yano.app-chain.members)` | The node's member key is not in the member list. | Fix `yano.app-chain.members` or the node's `signing-key`. |
| The node does not start: `… is not selected (available: […])` | The configured `state-machine` id does not match any loaded state machine. | Fix the id, or install the plugin bundle on that node. |
| The node does not start: `Retained state-commitment profile, fingerprint, or genesis id is incompatible` | The ledger on disk belongs to another identity. | Restore the original identity settings. Do not reset retained data; see [Chain identity](https://yano-x.io/concepts/chain-identity/). |
| The node does not start: `consensus quorums do not intersect in an honest member` | The threshold is too low for the member count and fault bound. | Choose a threshold `t` with `2t − n > f` and `t ≤ n − f`. See [Keys and trust](https://yano-x.io/concepts/trust-model/#how-many-members-can-fail). |

#### HTTP 429 or 503 on submit

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `429 … pending pool is full (10000 messages) — retry later` | The member's pending pool is full, 10,000 messages by default. Inbound gossip is dropped and counted too. | Retry with backoff. Raise `pool.max-messages` for the chain (it must be at least `block.max-messages`), or drain faster with a shorter `block.interval-ms` or a larger `block.max-messages`. |
| `503 Submissions are paused (admin)` | An operator paused submissions. | Resume them with the privileged `/admin/resume` route. |
| `400` with a code | The state machine refused the command at admission. | Fix the command; nothing was queued. |

#### A membership change is refused

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `400` with `MEMBERSHIP_QUORUM_INVALID` from `admin/members/add`, `admin/members/remove`, or `admin/threshold`; the message lists the thresholds that would work | The change would leave a `t`-of-`n` that cannot certify blocks: every epoch needs `2t − n > f` and `t ≤ n − f`, where `f` is `consensus.max-byzantine-members` (default 0). Adding a member keeps the current threshold, so 2-of-3 plus one member would be 2-of-4. | Change the threshold first, wait until status reports it in `membershipActiveThreshold`, then retry. For an application set up with the setup commands, `./yano.sh appchain approve` raises the threshold first for you, for example from 2-of-3 to 3-of-4. |
| `approve` says `No threshold suits both 1 and 2 members` | No threshold certifies both one and two members with `f = 0`. | Set the application up with more members instead. |

#### A member is stalled

A member stalls when a peer is ahead and it has made no progress for 60 seconds.
Its log shows `App chain '<id>' appears stalled: local tip …, best peer tip …`,
the node raises `AppChainStalledEvent`, its status shows `stalled`, the
`yano.appchain.stalled` gauge is 1, and the `appchain` health group reports it.

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| It cannot apply certified blocks because it computes a different state root | Look for `Catch-up block state-root mismatch` or `Proposal state-root mismatch` in its log. Fix the non-determinism, or deploy the same plugins and configuration as the other members (compare each node's `pluginCatalogFingerprint` from its chain `identity` endpoint), then restart it. |
| It cannot reach its peers | Check connectivity and the peer list; catch-up resumes on its own once a peer is reachable. |
| Its own view of Cardano is behind | Catch-up pauses until the block's Cardano reference is within its view; let its Cardano node sync. On a node set up with the setup CLI, the `Cardano:` line of `./yano.sh appchain status` shows `syncing: about N hours behind` until it is `up to date`. |
| It is far behind after a long outage | Let catch-up run, or restore a recent [snapshot](https://yano-x.io/concepts/recovery/#snapshots) and let it catch up the rest. |

Restarting a member is safe: finalized history is immutable and vote locks are
persisted. Never delete `appchain-chainstate/` to "fix" a stall; deleting
`appchain-indexers/` only rebuilds read indexes. See
[Restart, catch-up and snapshots](https://yano-x.io/concepts/recovery/).

# Tutorials
