## App Ledger Tutorials

Source: https://yano-x.io/tutorials/

> These tutorials are progressive, but each one can be used on its own. Every tutorial starts with its goal, what you will learn, what you need, and how…

These tutorials are progressive, but each one can be used on its own. Every
tutorial starts with its goal, what you will learn, what you need, and how long
it takes. Most end with a **Go deeper** section for the trust, consensus,
proof, or operational details.

Yano's tooling calls an app ledger an *app chain*, so commands and file names
say `appchain`.

| Tutorial | Level | Time | What you end with |
|---|---|---:|---|
| [1. Your first app ledger](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/01-first-app-chain/) | Beginner | 15 min, plus optional extras | Three members finalize the same event history |
| [2. Registry and proofs](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/02-registry-and-proofs/) | Beginner | 15 min | Owner-controlled data with an MPF proof |
| [3. Stock state machines](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/03-stock-state-machines/) | Beginner to intermediate | 20 min | The smallest built-in application model for your use case |
| [4. Evidence publication](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/04-evidence-publication/) | Intermediate | 30 min | S3, IPFS, and Kafka effects plus proofs and an anchor |
| [5. Domain-role approvals](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/05-domain-role-approvals/) | Intermediate to advanced | 30 min | Role-gated approvals, then the evidence specialization |
| [6. Webhook effects](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/06-webhook-effects/) | Intermediate | 20 min | A finalized decision invokes an external HTTP endpoint |
| [7. Anchors and verification](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/07-anchors-and-verification/) | Intermediate | 20 min | An application proof connected to a Cardano anchor |
| [8. Plugins and composites](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/08-plugins-and-composites/) | Advanced | 30–60 min | Yano extended without rebuilding or forking the host |
| [9. From demo to pilot](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/09-from-demo-to-pilot/) | Advanced | Planning session | A rehearsed multi-operator setup and a deployment plan |

Tutorial 4 and the evidence track of tutorial 5 use Docker Compose for their
services. Tutorial 8 also needs a Java build tool.

**Declarative bindings** have their own track:
[connect existing state machines without Java](https://yano-x.io/bindings/). It is
experimental and needs a Yano X build that includes the feature; its overview
explains which build to use.

#### Which build to use

Every tutorial runs `./yano.sh` from the top-level directory of an extracted
Yano X JVM distribution, the one containing `yano.sh` and `yano.jar`. Use a
[release download](https://yano-x.io/start-here/release-downloads/), or
[build the distribution from source](https://yano-x.io/start-here/build-from-source/) and extract
the archive it produces. The commands are the same either way.

These guides follow the current source. A feature added after your release
appears only after you build from source; when a command is missing, check
`./yano.sh appchain help` in your distribution.

#### Tutorial conventions

- Treat `./yano.sh` as the product command. The tutorials run their members
  with `./yano.sh appchain try`, which rehearses the real setup commands
  (`new`, `request`, `seal`, `join`, `start`, and `status`) on one machine,
  with three operators, alice, bob and carol, under `./appchain-try/`. To run
  an application with other operators, use the same commands; see
  [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/).
- Local devnet data is disposable. `./yano.sh appchain stop --node-dir …`
  preserves it; `./yano.sh appchain try --clean` deletes the rehearsal.
- `try` picks the first free HTTP ports from `8080` and node ports from
  `13337`, and prints them; each node's ports are also in its `node.json`.
  The showcase and the Docker-based tutorials use HTTP ports `7070`–`7072`,
  and the Evidence Explorer uses `7080`.
- Demo credentials are known or generated locally. Never reuse them outside an
  isolated development environment.
- A successful HTTP submission means "accepted for sequencing", not "already
  final". Wait for the block, or use the scenario verifier.
- A finalized command that breaks a business rule is a deterministic no-op.
  Always check the resulting state, not only the HTTP response or block height.
- Each tutorial marks the output to look for with **✓ You should see**.

#### Confidence levels used here

- **Shipped:** present in the current branch and covered by module tests.
- **Demo-proven:** exercised by the packaged multi-member demo and its
  connector and proof verification.
- **Preview:** useful for devnet, testnet, or a tightly controlled pilot, with a
  named production-hardening boundary.
- **Experimental:** not a production claim; follow its dedicated guide.

Use the [release capability catalog](https://yano-x.io/reference/capabilities/) to tell bundled,
first-party optional, reference, and experimental features apart before you
choose a tutorial path.

Return to the [start-here hub](https://yano-x.io/start-here/what-is-an-app-ledger/).

---

## Tutorial 1 — Your First App Ledger

Source: https://yano-x.io/tutorials/01-first-app-chain/

> Three members finalize the same ordered event, expose the same state root, and keep both across a restart.

To run this outcome with other operators, follow [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/).

- **Goal:** run three members on one machine and watch them finalize the same
  event.
- **You'll learn:** how a submission becomes final, what `members agree`
  means, how to get a proof for a message, and what a restart keeps.
- **Before you start:** an extracted Yano X JVM distribution, Java 25, `curl`,
  `jq`, and `python3`. The rehearsal picks the first free HTTP ports from
  `8080` and node ports from `13337`, and prints them. No earlier tutorial is
  needed.
- **Level:** beginner
- **Time:** about 15 minutes for sections 1–5. The optional extras add 10–15
  minutes.
- **Outcome:** three members finalize the same ordered event, expose the same
  state root, and keep both across a restart.

This tutorial uses Yano's self-contained Cardano devnet and the built-in
`ordered-log` state machine. It needs no external Cardano node, wallet, funds,
Kafka, or plugin.

Yano's tooling calls an app ledger an *app chain*, so the commands below say
`appchain`.

#### What you will see

Here is the whole tutorial in one picture. Each step shows the command you run
at that point. The "What if" scenarios show what happens when a member is down.

<!-- illustration: first-chain-finality -->
1. **Start.** `try` starts alice's node first. It produces the local devnet, is
   a member, and proposes the blocks. Then bob and carol start. The threshold
   is 2 of 3.
2. **Check agreement.** `status` reads each chain's status from every member
   and prints `members agree` when they report the same chain.
3. **Submit.** You send an event to bob's node. Bob's node signs the envelope
   with its member key and answers 202 with a message id.
4. **Gossip.** Bob's node shares the envelope with alice's and carol's nodes.
5. **Propose.** Alice's node, the proposer of `orders`, builds a block, applies
   it, and sends it with its PREPARE vote.
6. **Vote.** Bob's and carol's nodes re-execute the block and vote PREPARE,
   then COMMIT, only if their own state root matches.
7. **Certify.** Two COMMIT votes form the finality certificate, and every node
   commits the block.
8. **Agree again.** `status` prints `members agree` with a higher height.
<!-- /illustration -->

#### 1. Choose the working directory and start

Every tutorial runs `./yano.sh` from the directory that contains it. Choose one
setup.

From an extracted release, use its top-level directory, the one containing
`yano.sh` and `yano.jar`:

```bash
cd /path/to/extracted/yano-x-jvm-<version>
./yano.sh appchain help
```

From a source checkout, follow the
[Yano X distribution build](https://yano-x.io/start-here/build-from-source/), extract the JVM
archive it produces, and use that top-level directory. Yano X has no `:app`
task. For the curated thirteen-chain demo, use the
[showcase quickstart](https://yano-x.io/start-here/quickstart/) instead.

The remaining commands are the same for both setups:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain try
```

`try` runs the real setup steps on this machine and prints each command as it
runs it. A coordinator creates an application called `demo` with one chain,
`orders`, which uses the `audit-log` recipe: the `ordered-log` state machine.
Three operators, alice, bob and carol, each make a member key and a node
directory under `./appchain-try/`, and the coordinator seals the application.
Then each operator joins and starts their node:

- alice is the lead. Her node produces the local Cardano devnet, is a member,
  and proposes every block of `orders`;
- bob's and carol's nodes are members that follow alice's devnet.

With three members, the threshold is a majority: 2. Startup can take a few
minutes, because alice's node starts first and the others download its devnet
genesis.

> **✓ You should see** the numbered steps, then a message finalized at the
> same height and root on every node:
>
> ```text
>   alice  height 1  root 3d7d41336074db26…
>   bob    height 1  root 3d7d41336074db26…
>   carol  height 1  root 3d7d41336074db26…
> ✓ Message 53c00fd815014ae5… is final at height 1 on every node
> ```

Each node's HTTP port is in its `node.json`. Read the three ports into your
shell; the commands below use them:

```bash
ALICE=$(jq -r .httpPort appchain-try/alice/yano-node/node.json)
BOB=$(jq -r .httpPort appchain-try/bob/yano-node/node.json)
CAROL=$(jq -r .httpPort appchain-try/carol/yano-node/node.json)
echo "alice $ALICE  bob $BOB  carol $CAROL"
```

#### 2. Confirm agreement

```bash
./yano.sh appchain status --node-dir appchain-try/alice/yano-node
```

> **✓ You should see** `members online 3/3`, each member `online`, then:
>
> ```text
>   chain orders         height 1      members agree  members 3, 2 signatures  anchoring: not set up
> ```

`members agree` means every online member reports the same chain identity.
If two members report different state roots at the same height, `status`
also prints a warning that names the height. It is more than "three processes
are running", but it is a comparison, not a vote.

Open the status pages if you prefer a UI:

```bash
echo "http://127.0.0.1:$ALICE/ui/app-chain/"
echo "http://127.0.0.1:$BOB/ui/app-chain/"
echo "http://127.0.0.1:$CAROL/ui/app-chain/"
```

#### 3. Submit a business event

Submit through bob's node rather than through the proposer:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:$BOB/api/v1/app-chain/chains/orders/messages" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"topic":"orders","body":"{\"event\":\"order-created\",\"orderId\":\"A-1001\",\"quantity\":4}"}' \
  | jq .
```

> **✓ You should see** a JSON object with a `messageId`.

You did not sign anything. Bob's node checked the command, signed the envelope
with its own member key, and gossiped it. Alice's node put it in a block, two
of the three members voted for that block, and every member applied the same
bytes. The submission itself only means "queued on bob's node".

After a few seconds, inspect the finalized blocks and agreement:

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$ALICE/api/v1/app-chain/chains/orders/blocks" | jq .
./yano.sh appchain status --node-dir appchain-try/alice/yano-node
```

> **✓ You should see** a new block with `"messageCount": 1` and
> `certSignatures` of at least 2, then `chain orders` with a higher height and
> `members agree`.

#### 4. Capture a message ID and its proof

This time, submit through carol's node and keep the message id:

```bash
RESPONSE=$(curl -s -X POST \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$CAROL/api/v1/app-chain/chains/orders/messages" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"topic":"orders","body":"{\"event\":\"packed\",\"orderId\":\"A-1001\"}"}')

echo "$RESPONSE" | jq .
MESSAGE_ID=$(echo "$RESPONSE" | jq -r .messageId)
```

> **✓ You should see** a JSON object with `messageId`,
> `"chainId": "orders"`, and `"topic": "orders"`.

Wait until the message is final. A finalized message has a block height:

```bash
HEIGHT=0
for attempt in $(seq 1 30); do
  HEIGHT=$(curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$ALICE/api/v1/app-chain/chains/orders/messages/$MESSAGE_ID" \
    | jq -r '.height // 0' 2>/dev/null)
  [ "${HEIGHT:-0}" -gt 0 ] && break
  sleep 1
done
echo "final at height $HEIGHT"
```

> **✓ You should see** `final at height` followed by a number greater than 0.

Then request a typed proof that the message is recorded:

```bash
curl -s -X POST \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$ALICE/api/v1/app-chain/chains/orders/proof-subjects/finalized-message-v1/proof" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "$(jq -nc --arg id "$MESSAGE_ID" '
    {coordinates:{"message-id":$id}, view:"latest",
     claim:{claimId:"recorded",operands:{}}, includeEvidence:false}')" \
  | jq '{stateRoot:.proof.stateRoot,presence:.proof.presence,position:.fact.fields,claim:.claimResult.satisfied}'
```

> **✓ You should see** `"presence": "PRESENT"`, `"claim": true`, and a
> `position` with the message's `height`, `index`, `topic`, and `sender`.

The typed subject resolves the public message ID to its namespaced physical
state key and connects that record to the member's committed state root. The
`sender` is carol's member key, because carol's node accepted and signed the
envelope; `jq -r .publicKey appchain-try/carol/yano-node/node.json` prints it.
Tutorial 7 connects a state root to a Cardano anchor.

#### 5. Stop and restart

`stop` keeps both the L1 and the app ledger data. Stop the three nodes, then
start them again with the lead first, because the other nodes follow her
devnet:

```bash
for name in carol bob alice; do
  ./yano.sh appchain stop --node-dir appchain-try/$name/yano-node
done
for name in alice bob carol; do
  ./yano.sh appchain start --node-dir appchain-try/$name/yano-node
done
./yano.sh appchain status --node-dir appchain-try/alice/yano-node
```

> **✓ You should see** `✓ Stopped carol; its data is kept` for each node,
> then `✓ Node alice is up at http://127.0.0.1:…` for each node, then the same
> height and `members agree` as before the stop.

The retained heights and roots return unchanged before any new traffic is
finalized. Explore what each node keeps in its directory, for example
`appchain-try/alice/yano-node`:

<!-- illustration: node-directory -->

- `node.json`: the operator name, public key, addresses, and ports;
- `secrets/`: the member key and the node's API key;
- `apps/demo.chain`: the sealed application the node joined;
- `config/`: `consensus.yaml` and `node.yaml`, written by `join`, and
  `local.yaml` for the node's own settings;
- `data/`: `chainstate` (Cardano L1), `appchain-chainstate` (the app ledger),
  and `appchain-indexers` (rebuildable read indexes);
- `logs/node.log`: the node's log.

`appchain-try/coordinator/` holds the draft, the member cards, and the sealed
`demo.chain`. See [where each setting lives](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/#where-each-setting-lives).

This is a useful distinction:

- **restart:** the same chain identity and retained state;
- **`try --clean`:** delete the rehearsal; the next `try` seals a new
  application with a new identity and history.

The members and the threshold are sealed in `demo.chain`. To try different
values, rehearse in a new directory (see [Go deeper](#go-deeper)).

#### What you just proved

- A submission can enter through any member, and that member signs it.
- A threshold of members, not one REST server, finalizes the ordered block.
- All members deterministically derive the same state root.
- A message has a proof against that root.
- A retained restart recovers the same application history.

You did **not** yet prove Cardano settlement or the truth of the order fields.
Those are separate trust layers.

#### Optional extras

These sections reuse the running rehearsal. Skip them if you are short of
time.

##### A. Run a small `ordered-log` load test

The distribution includes the showcase's parallel load driver,
`examples/showcase/tools/loadtest.sh`. It finds members on consecutive HTTP
ports, starting at `YANO_SHOWCASE_HTTP_BASE`. `try` gives alice, bob and carol
consecutive ports when they are free; check that `$BOB` and `$CAROL` are
`$ALICE + 1` and `$ALICE + 2`. Start with a bounded workload of 500 messages,
10 concurrent submitters, and payloads of about 256 bytes, all sent to alice's
node:

```bash
YANO_SHOWCASE_HTTP_BASE=$ALICE examples/showcase/tools/loadtest.sh orders -n 500 -c 10 -s 256
```

Plain load-test mode suits any-bytes machines such as `ordered-log`. It
submits numbered UTF-8 bodies on the `load` topic, waits for the pending pool
to drain, and reports two different rates:

```text
==================== throughput ====================
  submitted attempts : 500
  accepted (2xx)     : 500
  dropped  (429 pool): 0
  errors             : 0

  SUBMIT rate        : ... msg/s
  finalized msgs     : 500   in ... block(s)
  FINALIZE rate      : ... msg/s
  end-to-end rate    : ... msg/s
====================================================
```

- **SUBMIT rate** measures how quickly an ingress REST API accepts messages.
- **FINALIZE rate** measures how quickly messages enter threshold-certified
  blocks; this is the meaningful chain-throughput measurement.
- **dropped (429 pool)** means backpressure worked because the pending pool
  filled. Reduce concurrency or tune the pool and block limits deliberately.
- **errors** are non-backpressure request failures and should be investigated.

Spread submissions across all ready members to exercise gossip from every
ingress path, then confirm that every member still agrees:

```bash
YANO_SHOWCASE_HTTP_BASE=$ALICE examples/showcase/tools/loadtest.sh orders -n 1000 -c 20 -s 256 --spread
./yano.sh appchain status --node-dir appchain-try/alice/yano-node
```

This is a functional throughput exercise, not a production benchmark. Results
depend on the machine, the JVM, the devnet producer, the block interval, the
payload size, and the member count. Record those inputs when comparing runs.
The test appends real finalized messages to the retained `orders` history.

For capacity settings and workload boundaries, see the
[`ordered-log` reference](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano/blob/main/docs/appchain/state-machines/ordered-log.md#operational-tuning).

##### B. Try an effect

An effect is an external action, such as a webhook call, that a state machine
commits as part of a final block and an executor node carries out.
[Tutorial 6](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/06-webhook-effects/) runs the full emit, delivery, result, and
proof lifecycle: a stock approval reaches its threshold and one node calls a
local webhook receiver. It needs its own rehearsal, so finish or clean up
this one first.

A production workflow should carry an explicit business id or finalized source
message id in its committed command or effect payload. The proof establishes
that the effect intent was committed; a real external action also depends on a
trusted executor and a verifiable receipt.

##### C. Governed member onboarding

The application is `governed`, so its members can add a fourth node, dave, on
the same host. These are the same steps as in
[grow and change your application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/add-chain/).

First, dave makes a key, a node directory, and a member card from the sealed
file. Choose two free ports for his node; the example uses the ones after
carol's:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain request appchain-try/coordinator/demo.chain --name dave \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --node-port 13340 --http-port $((CAROL + 1)) \
  --node-dir appchain-try/dave/yano-node --output appchain-try/coordinator --yes
```

> **✓ You should see** `✓ Wrote …/dave.member` with dave's key id.

Then every existing operator approves the card on their own running node.
Each `approve` waits until enough operators have approved, so on one machine
run the three in parallel:

```bash
for name in alice bob carol; do
  ./yano.sh appchain approve appchain-try/coordinator/dave.member \
    --node-dir appchain-try/$name/yano-node --heartbeat &
done
wait
```

With 2 of 3, a fourth member would leave 2 of 4, which cannot certify blocks
(a threshold must be more than half the members). `approve` therefore raises
each chain's threshold to 3 first and waits until that is active, then adds
dave and waits again, then restarts the operator's node once to connect to
him.

A change activates ten blocks after enough operators approve, and a chain
makes blocks only when it has messages. `--heartbeat` lets `approve` send
small heartbeat messages to an idle chain. On an `ordered-log` chain such as
`orders` each heartbeat is a permanent entry on the `appchain.heartbeat`
topic; your existing entries are unchanged. Without `--heartbeat`, send
ordinary traffic instead.

> **✓ You should see** `orders: first raising the threshold from 2 to 3 (4 members)`,
> then `✓ orders: dave is a member` and `Restarting this node to connect to dave …`
> from each operator.

When every operator has approved, dave joins and starts. `join` shows the
application and asks you to confirm the fingerprint:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain join appchain-try/coordinator/demo.chain --node-dir appchain-try/dave/yano-node
./yano.sh appchain start --node-dir appchain-try/dave/yano-node
./yano.sh appchain status --node-dir appchain-try/dave/yano-node
```

> **✓ You should see** `members online 4/4` and `chain orders … members agree
> members 4, 3 signatures`. The new member votes from the height at which
> the change activated.

A newly joined node accepts submissions only from that activation height on.
Before then, a submission through dave's node is refused with HTTP `503`
("not an active member at height ... yet"). Check a chain's
`memberActiveForNextBlock` field and retry once it is `true`:

```bash
DAVE=$(jq -r .httpPort appchain-try/dave/yano-node/node.json)
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:$DAVE/api/v1/app-chain/chains/orders/status" \
  | jq .memberActiveForNextBlock
```

#### Clean up

If you added dave, stop his node first: `try --clean` stops only alice, bob
and carol.

```bash
./yano.sh appchain stop --node-dir appchain-try/dave/yano-node   # only if you added dave
./yano.sh appchain try --clean
```

`try --clean` stops the nodes and deletes everything under `appchain-try/`,
including the chain identities.

#### Troubleshooting

| You see | What it means and what to do |
|---|---|
| `…/appchain-try already exists. Look around with …` | An earlier rehearsal is still there. Look at it with `status`, or remove it with `./yano.sh appchain try --clean`. |
| `The rehearsal stopped at that step (exit …)` | The command printed just above failed. If a node did not start, read the first error in its log, for example `appchain-try/bob/yano-node/logs/node.log`. |
| `members report different state roots at height …` from `status` | A node can be one block behind while `status` reads it. Run `status` again after a few seconds. If it persists, check that node's log. |
| `Port … is already in use by another program.` from `request` | Choose other free ports for dave with `--http-port` and `--node-port`. |
| `This node must be running; run  yano.sh appchain start  first` from `approve` | Start that operator's node with `start --node-dir`, then run `approve` again. |
| `orders: still waiting for …` and exit code 3 from `approve` | Not every operator has approved yet, or the chain has not made ten more blocks. Run the same `approve` again: it continues where it stopped. |

#### Go deeper

- **Try a stricter threshold.** The threshold is sealed in the application, so
  rehearse a second application in a new directory. A small template sets the
  threshold and the chain; `try --from` uses it:

  ```bash
  cat > strict.template.yaml <<'EOF'
  threshold: all
  chains:
    - id: orders
      recipe: audit-log
  EOF
  ./yano.sh appchain try --from strict.template.yaml --dir appchain-try-strict
  ```

  `seal` prints `3 members, 3 signatures per block`, and every block now needs
  all three votes. The "Threshold 3, one member down" scenario above shows why
  one stopped member then halts finality. If the first rehearsal still runs,
  `try` picks the next free ports. Remove this rehearsal when you are done:

  ```bash
  ./yano.sh appchain try --clean --dir appchain-try-strict
  rm strict.template.yaml
  ```

- Read Yano's
  [consensus guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano/blob/main/docs/APP_CHAIN_CONSENSUS_GUIDE.md)
  for the proposer, votes, certificates, replay, and catch-up.

**Next:** [Tutorial 2 — registry ownership and state proofs](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/02-registry-and-proofs/).

## Tutorial 2 — A Provable Shared Registry

Source: https://yano-x.io/tutorials/02-registry-and-proofs/

> Write owner-controlled data, show that an unauthorized write is a final no-op, and prove the current value with an MPF proof.

To run this outcome with other operators, follow [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/).

- **Level:** beginner to intermediate
- **Time:** about 15 minutes
- **Outcome:** write owner-controlled data, show that an unauthorized write is
  a final no-op, and prove the current value with an MPF proof.

This tutorial rehearses an application with one chain, `registry`, which runs
the stock [`kv-registry`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/kv-registry/) state machine
through the `owned-registry` recipe. The first member to write a key owns it;
only that member can update or delete it.

You need `curl`, `jq` and `python3`. Run every command from the top-level
directory of the extracted release, the directory that contains `yano.sh`.

<!-- illustration: registry-proofs -->
1. **Write as bob.** You write `supplier-42` through bob's node, so bob
   becomes its owner.
2. **Wait for the proof.** Poll the proof endpoint until the key is present.
3. **Write as carol.** Carol's node writes the same key. The message is final,
   but the decision is `KV_NOT_OWNER`.
4. **Compare.** The proven entry is unchanged; the state root has moved,
   because every block changes it.
5. **Update as owner.** Bob's node writes a new value, and the proof shows it.
<!-- /illustration -->

#### 1. Start a registry rehearsal

If Tutorial 1's rehearsal still runs, remove it first with
`./yano.sh appchain try --clean`. Then rehearse an application whose one chain
uses the `owned-registry` recipe:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain try --chain registry=owned-registry
```

> **✓ You should see** the numbered steps end with `members online 3/3` and
> `chain registry … members agree`.

#### 2. Create a registry entry

Each node's HTTP port is in its `node.json`. Read bob's and carol's ports into
your shell:

```bash
BOB=$(jq -r .httpPort appchain-try/bob/yano-node/node.json)
CAROL=$(jq -r .httpPort appchain-try/carol/yano-node/node.json)
```

The command body is CBOR. The tutorial helper builds it for you. Write through
bob's node, so bob becomes the owner:

```bash
TOOL=docs/appchain/tutorials/tools/stdlib_command.py
PUT_HEX=$(python3 "$TOOL" kv-registry put supplier-42 --value-text active)

curl -sS -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:$BOB/api/v1/app-chain/chains/registry/messages" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"topic\":\"kv-registry.command.v1\",\"bodyHex\":\"$PUT_HEX\"}" | jq .
```

> **✓ You should see** a JSON object with a `messageId`.

The message ID is bob's node's acceptance: the REST API answered HTTP `202`
and returned that ID. It means only that bob's node queued the message.
Wait until the key appears in a proof:

```bash
BASE=http://127.0.0.1:$BOB/api/v1/app-chain/chains/registry
KEY_HEX=$(python3 -c 'print("supplier-42".encode().hex())')

until curl -sf "$BASE/state/proof/$KEY_HEX" | jq -e '.presence == "PRESENT"' >/dev/null; do
  sleep 1
done
```

#### 3. Prove the current value

The state key is the UTF-8 business key itself:

```bash
curl -s "$BASE/state/proof/$KEY_HEX" | jq '{committedHeight, stateRoot, presence, valueHex}'
```

`valueHex` is CBOR `[owner, value]`: `82` opens an array of two, `5820` is
followed by bob's 32-byte member key, and `46616374697665` is the 6-byte
value `active`. The response also carries `proofWireHex`, an MPF proof that
this value sits under `stateRoot`. Showing JSON from one node is not
independent verification; a verifier checks the proof against a root it
trusts.

#### 4. Try an unauthorized write

Record the proven entry and the root, then write the same key through carol's
node, so you can wait for exactly that message:

```bash
ENTRY_BEFORE=$(curl -s "$BASE/state/proof/$KEY_HEX" | jq -r .valueHex)
ROOT_BEFORE=$(curl -s "$BASE/state/proof/$KEY_HEX" | jq -r .stateRoot)

PUT_HEX=$(python3 "$TOOL" kv-registry put supplier-42 --value-text suspended)

MESSAGE_ID=$(curl -sS -X POST \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$CAROL/api/v1/app-chain/chains/registry/messages" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"topic\":\"kv-registry.command.v1\",\"bodyHex\":\"$PUT_HEX\"}" | jq -r .messageId)

until curl -sf "$BASE/messages/$MESSAGE_ID" >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
curl -s "$BASE/messages/$MESSAGE_ID" | jq '{height, sender}'
```

The message is final at the printed height, sent by carol's node. Now compare:

```bash
ENTRY_AFTER=$(curl -s "$BASE/state/proof/$KEY_HEX" | jq -r .valueHex)
ROOT_AFTER=$(curl -s "$BASE/state/proof/$KEY_HEX" | jq -r .stateRoot)

[ "$ENTRY_BEFORE" = "$ENTRY_AFTER" ] && echo "entry unchanged"
[ "$ROOT_BEFORE" != "$ROOT_AFTER" ] && echo "state root changed"
```

You should see both lines. The entry did not change: carol does not own the
key, so the decision was `KV_NOT_OWNER`. The root did change, and it would
have changed anyway: every block also records its own messages root in state.
So compare the proven entry, never the root, to decide whether a command had
an effect. A final message, an accepted (HTTP `202`) submission, or a growing height is not the
authorization decision; the resulting state is.

#### 5. Update as the owner

Send the same `suspended` command, this time through bob's node:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/messages" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"topic\":\"kv-registry.command.v1\",\"bodyHex\":\"$PUT_HEX\"}" | jq .

until [ "$(curl -s "$BASE/state/proof/$KEY_HEX" | jq -r .valueHex)" != "$ENTRY_AFTER" ]; do
  sleep 1
done
curl -s "$BASE/state/proof/$KEY_HEX" | jq '{committedHeight, stateRoot, valueHex}'
```

The value now ends in `73757370656e646564`, `suspended`. The owner key is the
same.

#### 6. Clean up

```bash
./yano.sh appchain try --clean
```

#### Where this pattern fits

- allow-lists shared by several organizations;
- product, asset, credential or DID-document registries;
- shared configuration with explicit ownership;
- a current pointer whose exact value must be proved to a third party.

It does not provide organization roles, multi-party governance or document
indexing. Use [`authenticated-map`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/authenticated-map/),
the role workflow, or a plugin when the authorization is richer than “first
writer owns this key”.

#### Go deeper

- The [`kv-registry` reference](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/kv-registry/) covers
  configuration, typed proofs, Java encoding and design choices.
- Verify `proofWireHex` with the Java client and a trusted root instead of
  trusting the serving node; [Tutorial 7](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/07-anchors-and-verification/)
  connects a root to a Cardano anchor.
- Continue with [choosing a stock state machine](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/03-stock-state-machines/).

---

## Tutorial 3 — Choose a Stock State Machine

Source: https://yano-x.io/tutorials/03-stock-state-machines/

> Choose the smallest built-in deterministic model that matches your application, encode its commands, and configure a chain for it.

To run this outcome with other operators, follow [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/).

- **Level:** beginner for selection, advanced for wire integration
- **Outcome:** choose the smallest built-in deterministic model that matches
  your application, encode its commands, and configure a chain for it.

Selecting a state machine is a consensus decision. Every member must use the
same machine id and settings. For a new chain it is configuration; for an
existing chain, changing it needs a governed profile activation or a new chain.

#### 1. Answer three questions

<!-- illustration: sm-chooser -->

#### 2. Compare the stock machines

| Machine | Use it when | Who may change state | What a proof shows |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`ordered-log`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/ordered-log/) | You need one agreed order of opaque events | Any member's message | A message's height, index, topic and sender |
| [`kv-registry`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/kv-registry/) | You need mutable named records | The first writer of a key | Current owner and value per key |
| [`authenticated-map`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/authenticated-map/) | You need several collections with their own rules | Per collection: open, owner, member, role or approval | Status, revision and value digest per entry |
| [`approvals`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/approvals/) | Member nodes are the approvers | Distinct member keys | Status, approval count and payload hash |
| [`role-approvals`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/role-approvals/) | Approvers are business actors, not member nodes | Governed actors, organizations and roles | Policy outcome and payload hash |
| [`balances`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/balances/) | You need internal credits or netting | A minter mints; a member spends its own account | Balance per account |
| [`doc-trail`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/doc-trail/) | You need an ordered history per product or case | Any member appends | Entry count and chained head |

Two stock workflows are composites rather than single machines:

| Machine id | Use it when | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `composite` with `machines.composite.preset: evidence-v1-gated` | Approval coordinates S3, IPFS and Kafka publication | One root across components and effects; see [Tutorial 4](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/04-evidence-publication/) |
| `role-evidence` | The evidence flow needs business actors and roles | Governed actors, organizations and policies; see [Tutorial 5](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/05-domain-role-approvals/) |

#### 3. Encode a command

Stock machines read bounded, canonical CBOR commands. Use their Java contracts
or the tutorial helper; never serialize arbitrary Java objects.

<!-- illustration: wire-builder -->
1. **Write the command.** A `kv-registry` PUT is `[0, key, value]`.
2. **Encode.** The helper prints the canonical CBOR as hex.
3. **Admit.** The receiving member decodes it and answers `202`, or refuses it
   with `400`.
4. **Apply.** In the final block, the machine's rule decides what changes.
<!-- /illustration -->

Try the helper from the top-level directory of the extracted release:

```bash
TOOL=docs/appchain/tutorials/tools/stdlib_command.py

python3 "$TOOL" kv-registry put supplier-42 --value-text active
python3 "$TOOL" approvals propose release-7 --required 2 --payload-text go
python3 "$TOOL" balances mint alice 200
python3 "$TOOL" doc-trail product-42 abcd --reference ''
```

The command shapes are:

```text
kv-registry  [0, key, value]                                    PUT
             [1, key, h'']                                      DELETE
approvals    [0, itemId, payload, requiredApprovals, deadline]  PROPOSE
             [1, itemId] / [2, itemId]                          APPROVE / REJECT
balances     [0, account, positiveAmount]                       MINT
             [1, account, positiveAmount]                       TRANSFER from the sender's account
doc-trail    [entityId, entryHash, reference]                   APPEND; reference "" when none
```

`authenticated-map` and `role-approvals` carry signed actions and evidence; use
their CLI commands and Java authoring helpers described on their reference
pages. `ordered-log` takes any non-empty body.

#### 4. Choose the machine for each chain

When you set up an application, each chain names a *recipe*: a stock state
machine with the settings it needs. List the recipes and the answers each one
needs:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain recipes
```

| Machine | Recipe |
|---|---|
| `ordered-log` | `audit-log` |
| `kv-registry` | `owned-registry` |
| `authenticated-map` | `authenticated-map` |
| `approvals` | `approval-workflow` |
| `role-approvals` | `role-approval` |
| `role-evidence` | `evidence-ledger` |
| `doc-trail` | `document-trail` |

A machine without a recipe of its own, such as `balances`, uses the
`custom-plugin` recipe with its `stateMachine` answer. Read the machine's
reference page for the settings it needs.

To rehearse a choice on one machine, give `try` one `--chain <id>=<recipe>`
per chain. `new` takes the same options for a real application:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain try --chain orders=audit-log --chain workflow=approval-workflow
```

For more than a couple of chains, or for answers and settings, write the
chains in a small template and pass it with `--from`:

```yaml
### chains.template.yaml
chains:
  - id: orders
    recipe: audit-log
  - id: workflow
    recipe: approval-workflow
  - id: credits
    recipe: custom-plugin
    answers:
      stateMachine: balances
    settings:
      block.interval-ms: "1000"
```

```bash
./yano.sh appchain try --from chains.template.yaml
```

`answers:` fill in what a recipe asks for; `--answer <chain>.<name>=<value>`
does the same on the command line. `settings:` are flat chain settings that
`seal` fixes for every member; `--setting <chain>.<key>=<value>` adds one, and
`--without <chain>` leaves a template chain out. Settings that `seal` derives
from the draft, such as members, threshold, sequencing, and membership, are
refused there. A mistyped recipe or a missing answer stops `try` before
anything runs and leaves no rehearsal behind.

> **✓ You should see** `seal` list one line per chain with its recipe and
> genesis, for example `chain workflow approval-workflow genesis …`, and the
> final `status` show every chain with `members agree`.

`seal` writes every chain setting, including the state identity (commitment
profile, format fingerprint, and genesis id), into the sealed `<app>.chain`
file, and `appchain join` turns it into each node's configuration. You never
edit those files by hand, and no member can run different settings. To add a
chain to a live application, see
[grow and change](https://yano-x.io/deployment/add-chain/).

#### 5. Configuration is not arbitrary composition

Configuration selects and parameterizes semantics that already exist. It cannot
safely express new component order or terminal transitions, because those
change every member's state root. Use, in order of preference:

1. **stock configuration** when one machine or profile already fits;
2. **declarative bindings** when stock components must react to each other's
   events; see [declarative bindings](https://yano-x.io/bindings/);
3. **a composite plugin** when components need a new committed order or
   transition; or
4. **a custom state-machine plugin** for new business state or rules.

#### Common mistakes

- Treating a REST API key as an approval identity.
- Changing machine settings on one member only.
- Treating `202`, or a final message, as proof that state changed.
- Putting large or secret documents in replicated command bodies.
- Adding network, clock, DNS or random behavior inside `apply()`.
- Reusing a machine id after changing its deterministic behavior.

#### Clean up

If you ran a rehearsal, remove it:

```bash
./yano.sh appchain try --clean
rm -f chains.template.yaml
```

#### Go deeper

- [State machines](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/) lists every machine with its
  maturity, state key and proof subject.
- Each reference page, for example [`kv-registry`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/kv-registry/),
  covers REST, Java, proofs and design choices.
- The Yano [consensus guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano/blob/main/docs/APP_CHAIN_CONSENSUS_GUIDE.md)
  explains how blocks are ordered, re-executed and certified.
- For business actors, continue with
  [domain-role approvals](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/05-domain-role-approvals/); for coordinated
  publication, with [the evidence scenario](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/04-evidence-publication/).

---

## Tutorial 4 — Publish and Verify Immutable Evidence

Source: https://yano-x.io/tutorials/04-evidence-publication/

> Publish one immutable document through a threshold-approved workflow, preserve it in S3-compatible storage and IPFS, notify Kafka, and verify the chain…

To run this outcome with other operators, follow [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/).

- **Level:** beginner to advanced
- **Time:** about 30 minutes for the first build
- **Outcome:** publish one immutable document through a threshold-approved
  workflow, preserve it in S3-compatible storage and IPFS, notify Kafka, and
  verify the chain, connector, proof, and Cardano-anchor evidence.

This is Yano's most complete no-code vertical scenario. Docker Compose starts
three Yano members plus Kafka, RustFS (S3-compatible object storage), Kubo
IPFS, and the Evidence Explorer.

**Before you start:**

- You need JDK 25, Docker with Compose v2, `curl`, `jq`, `openssl`, and
  Python 3. The stack is tested with Docker Desktop. On Colima with a
  `virtiofs` mount, RustFS refuses its owner-only secret files and the stack
  rolls back ([#36](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/issues/36)).
- The harness ships in the extracted Yano X JVM distribution at
  `examples/evidence`. It finds the distribution's `yano.jar` by itself.
- It uses ports 7070–7072 for the members and 7080 for the Explorer, plus 9092,
  9000, and 5001 for Kafka, RustFS, and Kubo. A running showcase holds
  7070–7072; stop it first with `./showcase.sh stop` in `examples/showcase`.
  An `./yano.sh appchain try` rehearsal from earlier tutorials uses ports from
  8080 and 13337, so it does not clash, but you can remove it with
  `./yano.sh appchain try --clean`.
- The harness never moves a busy port. If another program holds one, export a
  free port before the first command and keep it set for the whole tutorial.
  `DEMO_HTTP_BASE` moves the members to that port and the next two, and
  `DEMO_UI_PORT`, `DEMO_KAFKA_PORT`, `DEMO_S3_PORT` and `DEMO_IPFS_PORT` move
  the other services. For example, `export DEMO_HTTP_BASE=7370` puts the
  members on 7370–7372, and the URLs the harness prints use those ports.
- `prepare` and every `up` build two local Docker images from the
  distribution. By default they are tagged `yano-adr013-node:local` and
  `yano-adr013-runner:local` (inside a Git working tree, the tag is that
  tree's short commit instead). Building **replaces any existing local image
  with the same name and tag**, for example one from another Yano X version.
  To keep other images, choose your own names before the first command and
  keep them set for the whole tutorial:

  ```bash
  export DEMO_YANO_IMAGE=yano-adr013-node:tutorial
  export DEMO_RUNNER_IMAGE=yano-adr013-runner:tutorial
  ```

The harness runs the default `evidence-v1-gated` profile, in which validator
members approve each release. The Studio link above opens the
`evidence-ledger` recipe, which selects the role-aware `role-evidence` profile,
where named business actors approve instead; the harness runs that profile
when you add `--machine role` to every command.

#### How one publication flows

<!-- illustration: evidence-pipeline -->
1. **Stage.** The runner stages the exact document bytes in RustFS and computes
   the IPFS CID.
2. **Approve.** It registers the document hash and records a member approval for
   the exact evidence command.
3. **Release.** `evidence.release.v1` records the version and emits `object.put`
   and `ipfs.pin` effects.
4. **Store and pin.** After finality, the effect owner archives the object and
   pins the CID.
5. **Incorporate.** Both results return to the ledger; status becomes
   `STORAGE_READY`.
6. **Notify.** A `kafka.publish` effect publishes the event; status becomes
   `READY`.
7. **Agree and anchor.** The runner waits for all members to agree and for a
   devnet anchor that covers the result.
8. **Verify.** It checks finality, the anchor, state and effect proofs, and the
   Kafka event.
<!-- /illustration -->

The source document itself is not put into consensus state. The chain commits
its business identity, version, hashes, workflow decisions, effect intents,
and acknowledged outcomes.

#### 1. Prepare and start a fresh direct-continuation profile

Run every command in this tutorial from the harness directory. From the
top-level directory of the extracted distribution, the one containing
`yano.sh`:

```bash
cd examples/evidence

./demo.sh prepare \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct

./demo.sh up \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct
```

`prepare` stages the plugins, runner, and images and generates private
configuration and keys. It ends with:

```text
Prepared compose demo instance 'tutorial-evidence'.
Secrets: <path> (values are not printed)
```

`up` starts the services, bootstraps the devnet script anchor, and runs a
read-only readiness probe. Near the end of its output, look for:

```text
PASS command=probe
...
Yano status: http://127.0.0.1:7070/ui/app-chain/ (nodes: 7070, 7071, 7072)
Evidence UI: http://127.0.0.1:7080/
API key file: <path>
```

`direct` means the deterministic workflow emits the next result-driven
transition directly. `explicit`, the harness default, keeps the first version
of this workflow, in which a separate notify command advances that
continuation. The choice is part of the fresh chain's committed profile; pass
the same option to every later command.

If startup fails, the launcher rolls back the partial deployment. Use the
reported container health/log command rather than repeatedly deleting random
directories; retained L1 and app ledger identities are deliberately checked.

#### 2. Publish version 1

```bash
./demo.sh publish \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id product-passport-001 \
  --sample-file samples/inspection-certificate.json
```

The runner waits for the whole dependency-ordered workflow shown above, from
staging to the anchor. On success it prints:

```text
PASS command=publish scenario=<scenario id>
```

On failure it prints `FAIL code=<CODE>` instead; for example,
`STORAGE_FAILED` when a storage connector did not confirm.

#### 3. Verify without changing anything

```bash
./demo.sh verify \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id product-passport-001 \
  --business-version 1
```

`verify` is read-only. It does not submit an app message, stage an object, pin
content, publish Kafka data, or force another anchor. It re-reads the immutable
object and IPFS content, checks their hashes, checks the Kafka acknowledgement,
and validates application finality, state/effect proofs, and anchor linkage.
It ends with `PASS command=verify scenario=<scenario id>`.

Open the Evidence Explorer at the `Evidence UI` address that `up` printed,
<http://127.0.0.1:7080/> by default (or your `DEMO_UI_PORT`), and select the
record. The JSON preview is a
bounded presentation copy produced only after the runner re-downloads and
verifies the external bytes; it is not the browser's original submission.

#### 4. Demonstrate immutability and versioning

An evidence version never changes. `publish` refuses an evidence id that
already exists with `EVIDENCE_ALREADY_EXISTS`, and the guided `run` command
stops with `REPUBLISH_REQUIRED`, before any connector write, when the bytes
differ from the retained version. To add a legitimate revision, create the
exact next immutable version:

```bash
./demo.sh republish \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id product-passport-001 \
  --business-version 2 \
  --sample-file samples/inspection-certificate-product-a-v2.json

./demo.sh verify \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id product-passport-001 \
  --business-version 1

./demo.sh verify \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id product-passport-001 \
  --business-version 2
```

Both versions remain independently selectable and verifiable. Any other
version number fails with `VERSION_CONFLICT`: the next version must be exactly
the latest plus one.

#### 5. Demonstrate idempotent replay

```bash
./demo.sh replay \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id product-passport-001 \
  --business-version 2 \
  --sample-file samples/inspection-certificate-product-a-v2.json
```

The replay envelope finalizes, but the accepted business record, effect set,
and logical external outcomes do not duplicate: the runner checks that the
record and the Kafka end offset are unchanged, then prints
`PASS command=replay scenario=<scenario id>`. A file whose bytes differ from
version 2 stops with `REPLAY_INPUT_MISMATCH`.

#### 6. Optional bounded parallel workload

Start small and use a fresh prefix:

```bash
./demo.sh load \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --load-mode pipeline \
  --count 8 \
  --concurrency 8 \
  --max-in-flight 8 \
  --id-prefix tutorial-load \
  --sample-file samples/inspection-certificate.json

./demo.sh verify \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id tutorial-load-000008 \
  --business-version 1
```

This measures a full workflow with approvals, external actions, proofs, and
anchors—not raw HTTP admission TPS. The load command prints `PASS` with a
summary when every item succeeded, and the Explorer shows the aggregate report.

#### 7. Stop and retain the scenario

```bash
./demo.sh status --instance tutorial-evidence --continuation direct
./demo.sh stop --instance tutorial-evidence --continuation direct
```

Run `up` with the same instance/profile to resume retained data. Delete data
only when you intend to retire that chain identity. Cleanup always names a
distinct replacement instance, so the retired chain id is never reused. To
retire this instance and also delete the shared devnet L1 it uses:

```bash
./demo.sh clean \
  --instance tutorial-evidence \
  --continuation direct \
  --scope all \
  --new-instance tutorial-evidence-next \
  --yes
```

`--scope all` refuses while another instance on the same devnet, such as
Tutorial 5's `tutorial-roles`, still uses the L1. Retire only this instance
and keep the L1 with `--scope instance` and the same `--new-instance` option.
The built Docker images are not removed; delete them with `docker image rm`
if you no longer need them.

#### What is and is not proven

The scenario proves that the approved bytes and connector outcomes are bound
to threshold-finalized application state and an L1 anchor. It does not prove
that an inspection statement is factually true, that an actor had a legal
credential, or that every future copy of a referenced document remains
available. Those require domain onboarding, custody, retention, and possibly
independent real-world auditing.

#### Go deeper

- Read the [plain-language evidence flow](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/docs/EVIDENCE_CHAIN_DEMO.md).
- Compare lifecycle and pipeline scheduling.
- Stop one member and exercise catch-up using the isolated E2E gate.
- Replace RustFS with a tested S3-compatible production service while keeping
  the `object.put` contract unchanged.
- Review the [optional connector packaging and security matrix](https://yano-x.io/deployment/connectors/)
  before translating the demo into a deployment.

Next: [domain-role authorization](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/05-domain-role-approvals/).

---

## Tutorial 5 — Generic Domain Actors and Role-Aware Approval

Source: https://yano-x.io/tutorials/05-domain-role-approvals/

> Run a release that business actors from different organizations approve under a governed policy, confirm that deliberate mistakes are final but count for…

To run this outcome with other operators, follow [Set up an application](https://yano-x.io/deployment/configure/).

- **Level:** application developer; advanced for identity governance
- **Time:** about 30 minutes, plus the first image build
- **Outcome:** run a release that business actors from different
  organizations approve under a governed policy, confirm that deliberate
  mistakes are final but count for nothing, and rotate and revoke an actor key.

Role-aware approval separates two identities:

- **member identity:** which member node relayed an envelope; and
- **actor identity:** which business actor signed the exact statement inside it.

This tutorial runs the evidence demo's `role-evidence` profile, which builds on
the same actor registry and approval rules as the generic
[`role-approvals`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/role-approvals/) machine.

#### How the policy decides

The demo's policy, `evidence-release`, needs a `manufacturer` to propose, two
`auditor` actors from distinct organizations, and one `regulator`. The demo
sends these statements for one release, in this order:

<!-- illustration: role-policy -->
1. **Manufacturer proposes.** `manufacturer-a` opens the proposal.
2. **Wrong role.** `manufacturer-a` tries to approve as an auditor:
   `ROLE_MISMATCH`, a final no-op.
3. **Wrong payload.** `auditor-a1` signs another hash: `CONFLICT`, a final
   no-op.
4. **First auditor.** `auditor-a1` from `audit-org-a` approves.
5. **Same organization.** `auditor-a2`, also from `audit-org-a`, approves:
   `DISTINCTNESS_DUPLICATE`, a final no-op.
6. **Second auditor.** `auditor-b` from `audit-org-b` approves; the regulator
   clause is still open.
7. **Regulator approves.** `regulator-a` approves, and the proposal is APPROVED
   with three accepted decisions.
<!-- /illustration -->

The three mistakes are final, like every other message, but they change
nothing. Only eligible, signed decisions count toward the policy.

The codes above are the decisions the machine makes, but it does not store a
code for each command, so the demo cannot print them. You see their result
instead: the approved proposal keeps only the three accepted decisions, and
`publish` fails unless they are exactly `auditor-a1`, `auditor-b` and
`regulator-a`. The [`role-approvals` reference](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/role-approvals/)
lists every code and the order of the checks.

#### 1. Start the role profile

You need JDK 25, Docker with Compose v2, `curl`, `jq`, `openssl` and Python 3.
The stack uses the same ports as Tutorial 4: 7070–7072 for the members, 7080
for the Explorer, and 9092, 9000 and 5001. If any is busy, export the same
`DEMO_HTTP_BASE` or other `DEMO_*_PORT` overrides that
[Tutorial 4](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/04-evidence-publication/) describes before the first command,
and keep them set for the whole tutorial.

From the top-level directory of the extracted release:

```bash
cd examples/evidence

./demo.sh up \
  --instance tutorial-roles \
  --machine role \
  --continuation direct
```

`up` prepares the instance first: it generates its secrets and builds the Yano
and runner images, which takes a while the first time. `./demo.sh prepare` runs
only that preparation, if you want to do it ahead of time. The images use the
same default tags as Tutorial 4 and replace local images with those tags; set
`DEMO_YANO_IMAGE` and `DEMO_RUNNER_IMAGE` as
[Tutorial 4](https://yano-x.io/tutorials/04-evidence-publication/) describes to keep them. Then `up`
starts three members and the publication services, and funds and bootstraps a
devnet anchor.

With `--machine role`, `up` then runs `init` rather than the read-only probe
of Tutorial 4. `init` writes to the chain: it submits governed messages that
register the four organizations, the five demo actors and the
`evidence-release` policy, and waits until they are final. It skips records
that already exist, so running `up` again does not register them twice.

> **✓ You should see** `PASS command=init`, and near the end the
> `Evidence UI: http://127.0.0.1:7080/` address.

The profile commits its organization and actor registry, policy, component
order, routes, effect workflow, administrator threshold and limits at genesis.
It is not a setting you can switch on for an existing chain. Pass the same
`--machine role --continuation direct` to every command for this instance.

#### 2. Publish actor-authorized evidence

```bash
./demo.sh publish \
  --instance tutorial-roles \
  --machine role \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id regulated-product-001 \
  --sample-file samples/inspection-certificate.json
```

The runner submits the statements shown above, including the three negative
controls, then releases the evidence once the proposal is APPROVED.

> **✓ You should see** `PASS command=publish scenario=regulated-product-001-...`.
> The run's report, which the Explorer in the next step shows, has an
> `APPROVED` authorization with three decisions: `auditor-a1` from
> `audit-org-a`, `auditor-b` from `audit-org-b`, and `regulator-a`.

#### 3. Inspect and verify

```bash
./demo.sh verify \
  --instance tutorial-roles \
  --machine role \
  --continuation direct \
  --evidence-id regulated-product-001
```

Open the Evidence UI at the address that `up` printed,
<http://127.0.0.1:7080/> by default, and select the record. Its **Business
authorization** card shows the decision status, the policy and its revision,
the proposer, each satisfied clause with its accepted and required counts, and
each accepted decision as actor, role and organization against a clause. It
also shows the payload hash and the relay member that carried the envelope.
The badges above it summarize what the runner verified, including
`Role quorum authenticated`.

The page shows the runner's verified report. It does not display the actor or
policy records themselves or their proofs; to inspect those, use the query and
proof routes on the [`role-approvals` reference](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/role-approvals/).

#### 4. Rotate and revoke an actor

```bash
./demo.sh role-lifecycle \
  --instance tutorial-roles \
  --machine role \
  --continuation direct
```

The exercise uses a dedicated recovery actor and checks, in order:

1. governed onboarding with proof-of-possession;
2. signing-key rotation;
3. the old actor revision and key are refused;
4. the new revision and key are accepted;
5. revocation;
6. refusal after revocation; and
7. proofs of the historical revisions and decisions.

> **✓ You should see** a few lines of output, among them
> `PASS command=role-lifecycle actor=recovery-probe revision=3
> rotation=verified revocation=verified ...`. The command checks every step
> above against proven state and stops with a `FAIL` line at the first one
> that does not hold; it does not print the steps one by one.

The other lines are expected: three `SLF4J(W): ...` warnings that the runner
has no logging backend, which you can ignore, and after the `PASS` line a
`WAIT_ANCHOR_ADOPTION: ...` line and an `Anchor binding verified ...` line
from the harness's anchor check.

This is not member rotation. Business credentials and member nodes are
governed separately.

#### 5. Stop and retain

```bash
./demo.sh stop \
  --instance tutorial-roles \
  --machine role \
  --continuation direct
```

`stop` keeps the instance's data and secrets.

#### Use the generic machine

The generic [`role-approvals`](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/role-approvals/) machine
approves any payload hash and emits nothing. Its reference page shows how to
set up an application with the `role-approval` recipe, sign statements with
`./yano.sh appchain role sign`, submit them on `role-approvals.command.v1`,
and query and prove the result. It also lists the lifecycle, the order of
checks and every outcome code.

Its organizations, actors and policies are created through member governance.
`./yano.sh appchain role bootstrap` encodes them from a role bootstrap plan.
`seal` writes that plan's template beside the sealed file as
`<chainId>.role-plan.yaml`; the reference page walks through filling it in
and the bootstrap, from actor keys to a read-back of every record.

#### Reuse levels

- **Configuration only.** Use a stock profile when its action and terminal
  transition already match. Governed data defines actors, organizations,
  roles, policies, counts, organization distinctness, deadlines and connector
  targets.
- **Small composite plugin.** Use the existing registry, approval, evidence or
  payment components in a new order, or connect approval to a different
  terminal action. Order and cross-component transitions affect consensus, so
  they stay reviewed Java composition.
- **Custom state-machine plugin.** Only for new state or business rules.

#### Production boundaries

- The demo uses deterministic actor seeds held locally. Production signing
  belongs in a KMS, HSM, vault or an actor-owned signing service.
- Yano proves that registered keys authorized exact bytes under a governed
  policy. Legal identity and real-world truth remain onboarding and audit
  duties.
- An actor record keeps at most 16 key epochs. Plan a successor identity before
  you reach that limit.
- Administrator authority is part of the profile; changing it is governed
  profile evolution, not an ordinary actor change.

#### Go deeper

- The [`role-approvals` reference](https://yano-x.io/state-machines/role-approvals/), with
  an interactive walkthrough of every outcome code.
- The complete [domain-role guide](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/docs/APP_CHAIN_DOMAIN_ROLES.md).
- The [evidence demo README](https://github.com/bloxbean/yano-x/blob/main/products/evidence/harness/README.md), for
  other profiles, ports and cleanup.
